emergency.heading: Antigua and Barbuda emergency number:
emergency.detail: Dial 911 or 999 in Antigua and Barbuda for police, ambulance, or fire. Royal Police Force headquarters: (268) 462-0125.
notices: Dial 911 or 999 for immediate emergency assistance in Antigua and Barbuda. UK government travel advice lists both numbers for ambulance, fire, and police.
To reach the Royal Police Force directly, the headquarters in St. John's is (268) 462-0125.

faqs.question: Is the emergency number in Antigua and Barbuda 911 or 999?
faqs.answer: Both. UK government travel advice lists 999 or 911 for ambulance, fire, and police in Antigua and Barbuda, and the Ministry of Health gives 911 as the emergency number. Both were checked on October 9, 2026.

faqs.question: Do emergency operators speak English?
faqs.answer: English is the official language of Antigua and Barbuda. We found no official statement on the languages emergency operators handle, so state your location and the help you need as plainly as you can.

faqs.question: Who do I call in Antigua after a theft or another crime?
faqs.answer: For an immediate threat, dial 911 or 999. Otherwise contact the Royal Police Force of Antigua and Barbuda: it publishes its headquarters, on American Road in St. John's, at (268) 462-0125. You can also report in person at a police station.

faqs.question: Does Antigua have a direct number for Emergency Medical Services?
faqs.answer: Yes. 911 and 999 remain the emergency numbers for ambulance, fire, and police. The Antigua and Barbuda police website also publishes Emergency Medical Services on 562-2432 and 562-2433 (area code 268).

faqs.question: I lost my passport in Antigua and Barbuda. Who do I contact?
faqs.answer: Report the loss to the police, then contact your own government's embassy, high commission, or consular agent. For US citizens, the State Department lists (268) 463-6531 as the main telephone of the US Consular Agency in Antigua; its page gives a separate after-hours emergency number, so note that one before you travel. For other nationalities, your government's travel-advice page for Antigua and Barbuda gives the current consular contact.

faqs.question: What number do I call in Antigua during a hurricane?
faqs.answer: For a life-threatening emergency, dial 911 or 999. The National Office of Disaster Services (NODS) publishes (268) 462-4206 on its website. The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June 1 to November 30: the US State Department singles out August, September, and October, and the Antigua and Barbuda Meteorological Service puts the peak in September.

faqs.question: What is the hospital in St. John's, Antigua, called, and what is its number?
faqs.answer: Sir Lester Bird Medical Centre, formerly known as Mount St. John's Medical Centre. It publishes (268) 484-2700 for physician details, clinic schedules, and general inquiries, and says its communication lines are for administrative inquiries: for a medical emergency it tells callers to dial 911. The hospital on Barbuda is the Hanna Thomas Hospital in Codrington. Check that your travel insurance covers medical evacuation.

essentials.advisory: As of May 20, 2026, the U.S. State Department lists Antigua and Barbuda at Level 1: Exercise Normal Precautions. Canada's advice, updated on May 26, 2026, also says to take normal security precautions. Neither means crime is absent: UK guidance records incidents of violent crime, including armed robbery and sexual assault. Check that your travel insurance covers medical treatment and evacuation before you go.

tips.label: Tap water
tips.text: Water: the U.S. State Department describes tap water in Antigua and Barbuda as generally safe to drink. The public utility, APUA, uses desalination; ask your accommodation whether its own supply comes from the mains or from a cistern or tank

tips.label: Sun
tips.text: Use sunscreen: the sun is strong in every month at this latitude, and strongest around the middle of the day

tips.label: Mosquitoes
tips.text: Mosquito repellent: pack it whatever the month, and read your government's health advice for Antigua and Barbuda before you travel

tips.label: At the beach
tips.text: The east coast faces the Atlantic, where the tourism authority describes powerful breakers at Devil's Bridge, although Long Bay on the same coast is protected by its reef. On any coast, UK travel advice warns that currents can be deceptively strong and that beach safety provision varies.

tips.label: On the road
tips.text: Taxis are not metered and standard fares are set by zone, so agree the fare and the currency before you set off. If you rent a car, remember that traffic drives on the left.

guides.title: Antigua Diving and Snorkeling Guide: Reefs and Wrecks
guides.summary: Antigua diving and snorkeling guide: Cades Reef, the Andes wreck, Stingray City, shore-snorkel beaches, PADI operators, courses, and when conditions are best.
guides.html:
Antigua pairs shallow fringing reefs you can swim to from the sand with historic wrecks and boat-access dive sites, in water warm enough to skip a thick wetsuit most of the year. You do not need certification to snorkel the reef off Dickenson Bay or the wreck of the Andes in Deep Bay, and if you do want to dive, PADI operators in English Harbour and Jolly Harbour run everything from a one-off Discover Scuba dive to full certification.

This guide covers the signature sites (Cades Reef, the Pillars of Hercules, the Andes wreck, and Stingray City), the best shore snorkeling beaches, operators and courses, seasonal conditions, and the reef etiquette and marine reserve rules that keep Antigua's water this clear.

What Makes Antigua Diving and Snorkeling Distinct

Antigua and Barbuda combine colorful fringing reefs, coral gardens, drop-offs, and well-preserved historic wrecks, with conditions gentle enough for first-time snorkelers and beginner divers. Antigua is particularly known for its wrecks, while Barbuda's sites see far less traffic. A shallow fringing reef rings much of Antigua, so good snorkeling is often a short swim from the beach, unusual for the Eastern Caribbean. Most dive centers cluster on the calmer south and west coasts, English Harbour and Falmouth on the south side, Jolly Harbour on the west, close to Cades Reef and the Pillars of Hercules.

Cades Reef: Antigua's Signature Barrier Reef

Cades Reef is a barrier reef running roughly two miles (about three kilometers) parallel to the southwest coast, off Cades Bay near Old Road, about a quarter mile offshore. It is reached by boat rather than by swimming from the beach, with most trips launching from Jolly Harbour and other west-coast points. Depth varies considerably, from shallow patches to much deeper sections, so operators can match a dive or snorkel to different experience levels on the same outing. Expect stingrays, lobster, parrotfish, surgeonfish, wrasse, and occasionally turtles.

The whole area, including mangrove wetlands, seagrass beds, and turtle-nesting beaches, was designated Cades Bay Marine Reserve in 1999, covering about 18 square kilometers under the Fisheries Division. Fishing, taking marine life, dredging, and discharging waste are all prohibited here without specific permission, protections intended to help the reef stay healthy.

One operator, Sea Cat Discoveries, runs a drift snorkel along the two-mile barrier reef (or an alternative shipwreck trip) on a 25ft Panga-style boat with pickups from most west-coast hotel beaches. As of 2026 the operator lists its three-hour Snorkel and Beach Exploration tour at about US$400 for one to four people, each additional person around US$75; confirm current pricing directly. Cades Bay Beach itself is calm for a swim, but the reef is well offshore, so reaching it means booking a boat.

Pillars of Hercules: A Boat Dive You Can Also Hike To

The Pillars of Hercules are eroded sandstone columns at the entrance to English Harbour, inside Nelson's Dockyard National Park below Shirley Heights. It is a shallow site, roughly 4 to 15 meters (13 to 50 feet), accessible to certified divers of all levels, and snorkelers are welcome too. PADI lists it as boat-access only, with local operators holding private moorings there. Marine life includes green turtles, spotted eagle rays, octopus, and reef fish such as trumpetfish and parrotfish, alongside a centuries-old anchor and a coral nursery program growing new coral since 2021.

There is also a land route, for the adventurous. From Galleon Beach at the mouth of English Harbour, walk to the end of the beach and around the point, then scramble over large, slippery boulders for roughly a 30-minute walk each way. Best attempted at low tide, and expect to get wet by the end; from the farthest walkable point, some visitors snorkel the rest of the way out to the pillars.

The Andes Wreck in Deep Bay: A Shore-Snorkelable Shipwreck

The Andes was a three-masted sailing barque built in 1874 that sank in Deep Bay in June 1905, after a cargo of pitch bound for Chile overheated and caught fire, forcing the ship into Antigua before it went down. It now lies upright in shallow water, roughly 8 to 10 meters (25 to 30 feet) deep, close enough to snorkel out to directly from the sand, one of the few shore-accessible wreck snorkels in Antigua. Deep Bay sits on the Five Islands peninsula and is nearly fully enclosed, so the water stays calm and clear, overlooked by Fort Barrington on the northern headland. The wreck and surrounding waters are protected under the Marine Areas Act of 1972, so nothing may be removed.

Stingray City: A Guided Encounter in the North Sound

Stingray City is a shallow sandbar in the North Sound off the northeast coast near Seatons village, reached by a short speedboat ride of about 5 to 10 minutes. Visitors usually stand in waist- to chest-deep warm, clear water while habituated southern stingrays glide around them, and guides teach safe handling: hold flat-palmed and never grab the tail. The sandbar is shallow enough to stand on, so non-swimmers can join too.

Most Stingray City tours add a snorkel over a nearby reef afterward, spotting parrotfish, sergeant majors, and occasionally turtles or starfish, plus rum punch after returning to the land base. Total time runs roughly 2 to 3 hours, and it is one of the more family-friendly water activities on the island; age limits and child supervision rules vary by tour, so check them when booking. Third-party listings put entry-level tours at roughly US$60 to US$70 per person as of 2026, combination tours closer to US$100; book directly to confirm current pricing.

These waters fall within the North Sound, a reef-sheltered cluster of islets, mangroves, and seagrass the site calls North Sound Marine Park, officially the Northeast Marine Management Area, a Marine Reserve since 2005 that also protects the critically endangered Antiguan racer snake and nesting hawksbill turtles. Great Bird Island sits inside the same zone. Conditions are calmest from December to April, and boat operators use mooring buoys rather than anchors.

Best Snorkeling Beaches From Shore

Not every good snorkel in Antigua needs a boat. These are the beaches where you can wade or swim out and see something worth the trip.

BeachShore snorkelWhat you will see
Deep Bay BeachYes, direct to the wreckThe Andes wreck, calm enclosed bay
Galleon BeachYes, reef just offshoreGreen turtles grazing seagrass, reef fish, occasional rays
Dickenson BayYes, fringing reef close to shoreColorful reef fish and coral in short swims from the sand
Green IslandBoat-access only, then shore-style snorkelClear water, coral, abundant fish on an uninhabited island
Cades Bay BeachNo, reef is well offshoreCalm swimming; book a boat for Cades Reef itself
Pigeon Point BeachLimitedCalm, shallow, family-friendly water rather than a snorkel highlight

Galleon Beach in Freeman's Bay is one of the best all-around picks, reached by a short boat ride or a scenic walk from Nelson's Dockyard, though road parking is limited. Dickenson Bay's coral fringe sits close to shore (the further-out spot locals call Paradise Reef needs a kayak or paddleboard, not a pure shore swim). Green Island, near Long Bay and Nonsuch Bay, is boat-access only but rewards the trip with an uninhabited island with no facilities.

Dive Operators and Certification Courses

Antigua's dive shops cluster around English Harbour and Jolly Harbour, running everything from a single Discover Scuba try-dive to full Open Water certification.

  • DiveCarib (English Harbour): called Antigua's only independent five-star PADI facility by the national tourism authority, with guided dive tours, certification courses, and technical diving for all levels.
  • Indigo Divers (Jolly Harbour): operating since 2005, run by PADI professionals, courses in English and German, dives on the sheltered west and south coast including Cades Reef, most sites about 20 minutes away.
  • Antigua Scuba School (Jolly Harbour, at Bodog Beach Club): founded by three instructors with over 30 years of combined teaching experience, instruction from beginner through professional level.

Not sure diving is for you? A PADI Discover Scuba Diving (DSD) session is the low-commitment way to try it: a non-certification dive for first-timers, minimum age 10, no experience needed, depth capped at 12 meters (40 feet), always supervised by a PADI professional. If you enjoy it, a full Open Water certification adds confined-water and open-water dives to the classroom work; at one operator (DiveCarib) the in-water portion runs about three days after separate eLearning. As of September 2026, that operator lists the Open Water practical portion at US$699, plus PADI eLearning of roughly US$246 to US$251 paid to PADI (the fee varies by country of residence), Advanced Open Water at US$529 for the dives plus about US$240 eLearning, and Discover Scuba at US$189; confirm current rates directly.

When to Go: Conditions and Seasons

Sea temperature ranges roughly 25 to 26C (77 to 79F) in the coolest months, December through February, up to about 28 to 30C (82 to 86F) in the warmest months, June through September, warm enough for most divers in a 3mm shorty wetsuit year-round.

Visibility is usually best from December through April: one local operator, DiveCarib, reports it is almost always above 18 meters (60 feet) and often around 30 meters (100 feet), though waves are on average higher in winter, which can limit site choice. From May through November seas are generally calmer (storms aside) and visibility is more variable; the same operator calls 9 to 12 meters (30 to 40 feet) a bad day, and notes that the tide cycle affects clarity more than the season.

Sargassum seaweed typically arrives May through August, peaking in June and July, affecting Atlantic-facing east-coast beaches most in heavy years, while Caribbean-side west and southwest beaches stay largely clear. It floats on the surface, so it mainly affects shore entry rather than deep-water visibility, but a heavy bloom is a real deterrent, so favor leeward west and south coast sites during peak bloom months.

Reef Etiquette and Safety

Antigua's reefs are fragile, and a few straightforward rules every diver and snorkeler should follow help protect them. Never touch, stand on, or step on coral: each polyp is a living organism, and even light contact causes lasting damage. Do not chase or grab marine life, including the stingrays at Stingray City, and expect boats to use a mooring buoy rather than an anchor over reef.

Non-nano mineral sunscreens (zinc oxide or titanium dioxide) are generally considered a lower-impact choice, though NOAA lists the nano forms of both among ingredients that can harm marine life, while chemical sunscreens containing oxybenzone, octinoxate, and octocrylene contribute to coral bleaching and are banned in some nearby jurisdictions, including the US Virgin Islands since 2020; Antigua has no formal ban of its own, but a rash guard and UPF swimwear cut down on reef runoff either way. Caribbean reef sharks and nurse sharks are present and regularly noted at several dive sites, both non-aggressive toward humans, with serious incidents anywhere in the Caribbean being rare. Lionfish, an invasive species, also turn up at some sites; avoid handling them because their spines are venomous.

These protections rest on the Marine Areas Act of 1972 and the Fisheries Act, under which both Cades Bay (1999) and the Northeast Marine Management Area (2005) were declared reserves. Inside them, fishing, taking marine life, dredging, discharging waste, unauthorized construction, and reef-damaging anchoring are all prohibited, with fines and other penalties for violations.

Diving and Snorkeling on Barbuda

Barbuda has little to no dedicated dive infrastructure, with no full-service dive shop on the island, so divers need to bring or arrange their own gear. It has a reputation for historic shipwrecks and very clear water, with Palmetto Point and Plasterer Point reported as worthwhile snorkel spots, though treat these as word-of-mouth rather than documented sites. Sea Bridge Ferries, formerly Barbuda Express, operates crossings in about 90 minutes each way using catamaran and monohull vessels, and a typical Barbuda day trip pairs the frigate-bird colony with beach time to swim or snorkel, so snorkeling here is opportunistic and beach-based. For serious diving, Antigua's own operators give a far more complete experience.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Antigua better for diving or snorkeling?

Antigua works well for both. Certified divers get boat-access sites like the Pillars of Hercules and Cades Reef, while snorkelers reach genuinely good reef and wreck sites directly from shore at beaches like Deep Bay and Dickenson Bay. Few Eastern Caribbean islands offer that much shore snorkeling alongside a developed dive scene.

Can beginners go scuba diving in Antigua?

Yes. A PADI Discover Scuba Diving session lets first-timers try a supervised dive with no certification or experience required, minimum age 10, depth capped at 12 meters (40 feet). If you enjoy it, the same operators run full PADI Open Water certification courses combining online learning with in-water training over about three days.

Do you need a boat to snorkel in Antigua?

Not always. The Andes wreck in Deep Bay and the fringing reef at Dickenson Bay are both snorkelable directly from the beach. Other standout sites, including Cades Reef and Green Island, are boat-access only, and the Pillars of Hercules can be reached by boat or on foot from Galleon Beach followed by a short snorkel.

When is underwater visibility best in Antigua?

Visibility is generally best from December through April, when local operator DiveCarib reports it almost always exceeds 18 meters (60 feet) and often reaches about 30 meters (100 feet), although winter seas tend to be rougher. From May through November the sea is usually calmer and diving remains good, with more variable visibility; even a poor day is typically 9 to 12 meters (30 to 40 feet).

Are there sharks in the water around Antigua?

Yes, Caribbean reef sharks and nurse sharks are regularly noted at several dive sites, but both are non-aggressive toward humans and serious incidents anywhere in the Caribbean are rare. Most divers who see a shark in Antigua describe it as a distant, uneventful sighting.

Is Stingray City safe, and can non-swimmers join?

Stingray City takes place on a shallow sandbar in the North Sound where you usually stand in waist- to chest-deep water, so non-swimmers can participate. Guides teach safe handling: hold the rays flat-palmed and never grab the tail. Minimum ages vary by tour operator, so confirm the policy for your booking; it remains one of the more accessible water experiences on the island.

Does sargassum seaweed affect diving and snorkeling in Antigua?

It can, mainly on Atlantic-facing east-coast beaches in the peak bloom months of June and July, affecting shore entry more than underwater visibility. Caribbean-side west and southwest sites, including those near Jolly Harbour and English Harbour, tend to stay largely clear, so favor those areas during sargassum season.

How long should I wait to fly after diving in Antigua?

PADI and the Divers Alert Network recommend waiting at least 12 hours after a single no-decompression dive before flying, and at least 18 hours after repetitive or multi-day diving. Plan your last dive with your departure flight time in mind, especially if you are diving right up until the end of a trip.

guides.title: Getting Around Antigua: Taxi Fares, Car Hire, Bus Routes
guides.summary: Fixed taxi fares by route, rental-car costs and the temporary driving permit rule, plus where the bus actually goes. Whether you need a car in Antigua.
guides.html:
Antigua is small enough that most point-to-point trips take 45 minutes or less, but you still face a real choice: rent a car and drive on the left, take a taxi at government-fixed rates, ride the informal private bus network, or mix all three. We found no official confirmation that Uber or Bolt operate here, though a homegrown app called Swyft Taxi has changed how you can book a ride. This guide covers what taxis and buses cost, what a rental car and its permit involve, how to reach Barbuda, and which areas you can cover on foot, with current fares and rules as of 2026.

The short version: staying mostly in one resort area with occasional taxis, you do not need a car. Chasing multiple beaches across the island in a single day, a rental car earns its cost quickly.

Getting around Antigua at a glance

Antigua covers about 108 square miles (281 sq km), small enough that most journeys run 45 minutes or under, with the busiest traffic between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. Here is how the main options compare.

OptionBest forTypical costWatch out for
TaxiAirport transfers, nights out, one-off tripsFixed fares, roughly US$15 to US$70Cash-based, agree the fare first
Rental carMulti-beach days, independent exploringRoughly US$35 to US$85+/day plus a US$20 permitLeft-hand driving, potholes, speed bumps
Public busBudget travel between St John's and townsRoughly US$0.85 to US$2 one wayNo fixed timetable, sparse Sundays
Swyft Taxi appOn-demand rides with upfront fareShown in-app before bookingStill building islandwide coverage
Barbuda Express ferryDay trips or stays on BarbudaUS$65 one way / US$120 round trip (adult)90-minute crossing, limited departures

Arriving at V.C. Bird International Airport

Every international flight lands at V.C. Bird International Airport (ANU), just north of St. John's. There is no public bus into the terminal, so your options are a taxi, a rental car, or a pre-arranged pickup.

Since December 1, 2025, the Antigua and Barbuda Airport Authority (ABAA) restricts who can collect paying passengers for hire to ABAA-approved taxis, rental companies, and tour operators. Family and friends can still collect you, and Fast Track hotels can collect registered guests, but an Airbnb host cannot without an approved permit, so confirm your pickup plan ahead.

In February 2026, the ABAA opened an expanded car rental and tour hub in the airport's old terminal (Terminal B), housing four rental companies with a combined fleet of around 315 vehicles, plus nine tour operators. Airport taxis run through two named associations, Mill Reef Taxi Association and United Taxi Association, with drivers uniformed and badged.

Taxis and Swyft Taxi: fares and how to book

Antigua taxis run on fixed, government-set rates rather than meters. Licensed taxis carry yellow plates marked "TX" (buses carry yellow "BUS" plates), a quick way to confirm you are in a licensed vehicle.

What a taxi from the airport costs

An older official schedule from 2005 lists low per-car figures some calculators still echo; current operator quotes run meaningfully higher. Treat the ranges below as spanning that old floor to what operators actually charge, and confirm the exact fare at the airport dispatch desk before you get in:

  • To St. John's: roughly US$15 to US$31
  • To the Dickenson Bay area and other northern resorts: roughly US$15 to US$45
  • To Jolly Harbour: roughly US$40 to US$60
  • To English Harbour and Nelson's Dockyard, the furthest point south: roughly US$45 to US$70

Fares are quoted per car for up to four passengers, so a solo traveler pays the same as a group of four; confirm the extra-passenger charge before boarding. Standard surcharges: waiting time about EC$12 (roughly US$5) per half hour, luggage beyond four pieces at EC$2.50 each, passengers beyond four at 25% of the fare each, and a 50% night surcharge from 10:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m.

Drivers accept US and Eastern Caribbean dollars (pegged at EC$2.70 to US$1); most street-hailed taxis are cash-only, with cards limited to the airport desk or pre-booked rides. A 10 to 15% tip is customary, and many drivers double as informal tour guides.

Swyft Taxi: the local ride-hailing app

We found no official source confirming that Uber or Bolt operate here. What the island does have is Swyft Taxi, a homegrown app that launched during Antigua Carnival in 2025. You book through the iOS or Android app, track your driver by GPS, see the fare upfront, and pay cashless. Every driver must hold a certified taxi permit, so it will not connect you with an unlicensed vehicle. Swyft works alongside traditional taxis and does not publish a fixed rate card, since fares are calculated and shown in-app before you book.

Public buses: cheap and informal

Antigua's bus network is privately owned minibuses and vans, typically seating around 15, running routes assigned by the government. Two hubs anchor it in St. John's: the West Bus Station on Market Street, serving the south and west, and the East Bus Station near the Botanical Gardens, serving the east.

The standout route for visitors is route 17, running from the West Bus Station to English Harbour, terminating at Nelson's Dockyard, roughly US$1.50 to US$2 one way, the best-value route to the south coast without a car. A bus also connects the West Bus Station with Jolly Harbour at a similarly low fare, though the exact route number is unconfirmed, so ask at the station for the next departure that way.

  • Buses run roughly 5:30 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. daily, no overnight service, and Sunday service sharply reduced.
  • No fixed timetable: minibuses leave when full, at the driver's discretion.
  • Fares run roughly EC$2.25 to EC$4.25 (about US$0.85 to US$1.60) one way, higher for late travel.
  • Buses generally skip the airport and northern hotel belt, connecting St. John's with residential villages, not tourist zones.

For a budget visitor near St. John's, route 17 plus a short taxi or hike from the dockyard reaches Nelson's Dockyard and Shirley Heights cheaply. Our budget guide covers more ways to stretch your money.

Renting a car: the permit, the cost, and the left-hand drive

A rental car gives the most freedom to string together multiple beaches and towns in a single day, hard to do on the bus network. First, though, you need a temporary local permit.

The temporary driving permit

Most visitors need a temporary local driving permit, although visiting residents of OECS Member States may be exempt. For visitors who need one, the temporary local permit costs EC$50 (about US$20), valid three months, easiest arranged through your rental agency at pickup when you hand over your home licence; it is also available at specific police stations or the Transport Board. Keep both licences in the vehicle, since police can ask to see them.

What a rental car costs

Expect roughly US$35 to US$55 per day for a compact or economy car, sometimes US$28 to US$35 booked well ahead. Economy SUVs average closer to US$55, standard SUVs US$75 to US$85. October tends cheapest (SUVs around US$66/day), December typically priciest. These are aggregator averages, not fixed rates, so prices vary by company and season.

Driving on the left

Antigua drives on the left, a holdover from British rule, and most rental cars are right-hand drive.

  • Roundabouts run clockwise, UK-style; give way to traffic already on the roundabout.
  • Speed limits run about 20 mph in towns and 40 mph elsewhere.
  • Main roads are paved but potholed even on major routes; secondary roads have frequent speed bumps and rougher stretches.
  • Goats, cattle, chickens, and dogs wander onto unfenced roads often, especially rurally.

Parking is generally easy outside the busiest pockets of St. John's and the marina areas, which fill on cruise-ship days. If left-hand driving worries you, a taxi or a pre-booked driver for the day is a reasonable alternative.

Getting to Barbuda: ferry or short flight

Barbuda, Antigua's low-lying sister island to the north, is reached only by ferry or a short flight, not by road.

The Barbuda Express ferry takes about 90 minutes each way, departing from Jolly Harbour Marina at the dock in front of Sea Dream Restaurant. As of July 2026, adult fares are EC$325 (US$120) round trip or EC$175 (US$65) one way, with lower child fares for ages 0-2 and 3-11. Baggage is limited to two pieces per fare-paying passenger plus a personal bag.

The ferry runs daily, but departure times vary by day and some sailings require an overnight stay. Check the operator's current timetable before booking. The operator currently lists no scheduled cargo trips. Weather can delay crossings, so build in flexibility, and check our Barbuda travel guide for what to do once you arrive.

BMN SVG Airways advertises daily flights to Barbuda International Airport from Antigua. Check the current fare and flight time with the carrier before booking. Once on Barbuda, there is no public bus network: arrange transport through your accommodation, a local taxi, or a rental.

Boat transport on the south coast

Around Nelson's Dockyard in English Harbour, a small water taxi crosses the harbor between the Copper and Lumber Store Historic Inn and Galleon Beach, a few minutes and up to about 10, roughly hourly on demand. Expect around US$4 each way, roughly US$6 to US$8 round trip, confirmed on the spot.

To reach Shirley Heights from Nelson's Dockyard, there is no local bus for that short but steep hop. A taxi runs roughly US$10 each way, or hike up from sea level; some take the water taxi to Galleon Beach first and hike up from there instead.

Day sails and catamaran day cruises run out of both Jolly Harbour and English Harbour. Operator names and prices change often, so our catamaran day cruise page is the better place to check current options.

What you can walk, and what you cannot

Antigua rewards walking in some pockets and punishes it in others.

  • St. John's: The cruise-port core is compact and walkable. Redcliffe Quay, Heritage Quay, the cathedral, the markets, and the shops sit within a short flat walk of the cruise berths. Sidewalks are inconsistent or absent outside that core.
  • English Harbour: The English Harbour and Falmouth Harbour visitor areas sit within easy walking distance of each other, and Falmouth Harbour's east side is a short walk from Nelson's Dockyard.
  • Jolly Harbour and Dickenson Bay: Both are self-contained resort and marina areas, walkable around your accommodation, but not within walking distance of each other or of St. John's. The coastal walk from Runaway Bay to southern Dickenson Bay runs about 30 to 40 minutes.

The takeaway: walk freely inside your resort area or the St. John's waterfront, and taxi, drive, or bus between areas. Our first-timers guide and cruise port guide build this into fuller day plans.

Which option fits your trip

  • One resort area, occasional trips out: taxis or Swyft Taxi cover you well; skip the rental and permit entirely.
  • St. John's and English Harbour without a car: route 17 handles that leg; pair it with taxis for the last mile to Shirley Heights or a beach.
  • Multiple beaches and towns over several days: rent a car. Our sailing and yachting guide covers the kind of flexible, self-driven trip that rewards it.
  • Adding Barbuda: book the ferry from Jolly Harbour ahead for the lower cost, or the short flight if your schedule is tight. See our Nelson's Dockyard and English Harbour guide for what to pair with a south-coast base.

Whichever mix you choose, the island's small size works in your favor: even a mistimed taxi or a missed bus rarely costs more than an hour.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there Uber in Antigua?

Not that we could confirm: no official source says Uber, Bolt or a similar international app operates in Antigua and Barbuda. For app-based booking, the island has a homegrown app called Swyft Taxi, which launched in 2025: you book in-app, see the fare upfront, track your driver by GPS, and pay cashless. Traditional street-hailed and dispatched taxis, running on fixed government rates, remain the main on-demand option.

Do buses go to the beaches in Antigua?

Mostly no. The bus network connects St. John's with residential villages and towns rather than tourist beach zones, and buses generally skip the airport and the northern resort belt. The exception is route 17, running from the West Bus Station to Nelson's Dockyard in English Harbour, useful if your beach plan includes the south coast.

How much is a taxi from the airport to my hotel?

It depends on distance. Approximate current fares run roughly US$15 to US$31 to St. John's, US$15 to US$45 to Dickenson Bay, US$40 to US$60 to Jolly Harbour, and US$45 to US$70 to English Harbour, quoted per car for up to four passengers. Confirm the exact fare at the dispatch desk before you get in, since rates vary by operator.

Do I need to rent a car in Antigua?

Not necessarily. If you plan to stay mostly in one resort area and take occasional taxis, you can comfortably skip the rental car. If you want to independently explore multiple beaches and towns over several days, a rental car offers far more freedom than buses or repeated taxi fares, at the cost of a temporary driving permit and adjusting to left-hand driving.

Is driving in Antigua hard for visitors?

It is manageable but takes adjustment. You drive on the left in a mostly right-hand-drive car, roundabouts run clockwise UK-style, and you need a temporary driving permit (EC$50, about US$20, valid three months) from your rental agency, a police station, or the Transport Board. Main roads are paved but can have potholes, secondary roads have speed bumps, and livestock often wanders onto rural roads.

How do I get from Antigua to Barbuda?

Two options: the Barbuda Express ferry, a 90-minute crossing from Jolly Harbour Marina running daily (from EC$175 one way for adults), or a flight to Barbuda International Airport. BMN SVG Airways advertises daily Barbuda flights; confirm current fares and flight times before booking.

What is the water taxi at Nelson's Dockyard?

It is a short boat crossing, a few minutes and up to about 10 minutes, connecting the dock at the Copper and Lumber Store Historic Inn in Nelson's Dockyard to Galleon Beach across the harbor. It runs roughly hourly on an on-demand basis and costs around US$4 each way. It is a convenient way to reach the beach without walking or arranging a taxi around the harbor.

Do I need cash for taxis and buses in Antigua?

Yes, mostly. Street-hailed and dispatched taxis are generally cash-only, accepting both US dollars and Eastern Caribbean dollars, with cards typically limited to the airport taxi desk or rides booked in advance. Public buses are also cash-paid to the driver. Swyft Taxi is the exception, since it takes cashless in-app payment. Carry small bills for taxis, tips, and bus fares.

guides.title: Antigua All-Inclusive Resorts: How to Choose Your Area
guides.summary: Antigua all-inclusive resorts differ by area: five main zones from calm Dickenson Bay to sailing-town English Harbour, plus a quieter east coast, matched to family or adults-only stays.
guides.html:
An all-inclusive in Antigua is less about the brand on the gate and more about which stretch of coast you wake up on. The island has 365 beaches and roughly a dozen resort zones, and they are genuinely different: a calm family bay in the northwest feels nothing like the sailing-town energy of the south. Pick the right area first, then the right property, and the whole trip falls into place. This guide compares Antigua's main all-inclusive areas by who they suit, then explains what "all-inclusive" actually covers here and how to choose between adults-only and family resorts.

We deliberately talk about areas rather than naming specific resorts, because properties change hands, rebrand, and renovate. The bay, the beach, and the drive times do not. Match those to your trip and you will be happy whichever sign is over the lobby.

The main all-inclusive areas at a glance

Most of Antigua's all-inclusives sit in one of five zones, with a further cluster on the east coast around Long Bay and Devil's Bridge that is worth knowing about if you want real quiet. Here is the quick version before we go deeper:

  • Dickenson Bay: the busiest beach strip in the northwest; calm water, lots of resorts, easy day trips.
  • Five Islands: quieter peninsula just west of the capital with a cluster of beach resorts and sunset-facing bays.
  • Jolly Harbour: a marina village on the west coast with shops, restaurants, and a long swimming beach next door.
  • Hodges Bay: a sheltered north-coast pocket near the airport, low-key and convenient.
  • English Harbour: the historic sailing south, built around Nelson's Dockyard and a more grown-up scene.

Antigua is small. You can drive coast to coast in well under an hour, so even a "quiet" base never traps you. Read our getting around Antigua notes before you decide whether to add a rental car, and remember that you drive on the left here.

Northwest: Dickenson Bay and Five Islands

The northwest is where most first-time visitors land, and for good reason. The beaches face west and northwest, so the water is usually calm and the sunsets are reliable.

Dickenson Bay: easy, social, well connected

Dickenson Bay is the island's most developed beach strip. Dickenson Bay Beach is a long arc of soft sand with gentle, swimmable water and plenty of watersports, beach bars, and boat operators working the shore. This is the area to choose if you want to walk out of your resort and immediately have things to do without organizing anything.

It is also the most convenient base for exploring. You are close to the capital, St. John's, for the cathedral, the national museum, and the cruise-pier shops, and within easy reach of Runaway Bay Beach and Fort James Beach for a change of scene. Day boats to Stingray City and catamaran cruises pick up nearby.

The trade-off is that Dickenson Bay is the liveliest, least secluded area. If your priority is a quiet, private-feeling beach, look further out.

Five Islands: quieter, west-facing, still close to town

Just west of St. John's, the Five Islands peninsula holds a small cluster of beach resorts on calm, sheltered bays. Galley Bay Beach, Hawksbill Beach, and Deep Bay Beach are the headline strands, and they feel noticeably more private than Dickenson Bay while keeping you only a short drive from the capital. Deep Bay even has a shipwreck you can snorkel to from shore.

Choose Five Islands if you want the convenience of the northwest with a calmer, more romantic feel. It suits couples and anyone who plans to relax on the resort beach most days and pop into town when the mood strikes.

West coast: Jolly Harbour and the sunset beaches

The west coast trades the northwest's density for long, open beaches and some of the best swimming water on the island. This is prime dry-season territory, with sun setting straight over the sea.

Jolly Harbour: village convenience plus a great beach

Jolly Harbour is built around a marina and has something most resort areas lack: a self-contained village with a supermarket, restaurants, bars, and a golf course. Jolly Beach next door is one of Antigua's longest swimming beaches. The area suits travelers who like an all-inclusive base but also want the option to walk out for an independent dinner or stock a villa fridge.

Jolly Harbour is also the gateway to the west coast's string of excellent public beaches. Ffryes Beach, Darkwood Beach, Valley Church Beach, and Turners Beach are all a short drive south, each with calm, clear water and a beach bar or two. It is an easy area to base a beach-hopping trip, and a natural launch point for a Barbuda day trip to see the pink sand.

South: English Harbour and the sailing scene

The south coast is Antigua's most distinctive base, and it is where the island's history lives. English Harbour is the heart of the Caribbean sailing world, anchored by Nelson's Dockyard, a restored Georgian naval base that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the centerpiece of Nelson's Dockyard National Park.

Resorts here lean upscale and grown-up rather than mega-resort. You stay among superyachts, historic stone buildings, and hillside restaurants, with the famous Sunday-evening party at Shirley Heights a short drive up the hill. The beaches are smaller and more tucked away, like Galleon Beach and Pigeon Point Beach, but the atmosphere is unmatched if you care about character over a wide resort strand.

This is the area to choose if you are a sailor or sailing-curious, if you want excellent restaurants off the resort, or if you are timing a trip around an event like Antigua Sailing Week (April 22–26 in 2026; April 21–25 in 2027) or the Classic Yacht Regatta. It pairs naturally with the scenic Fig Tree Drive and the Wallings Nature Reserve in the interior.

North coast: Hodges Bay and airport-close stays

The stretch of north coast near V.C. Bird International Airport, including Hodges Bay, is the most convenient area for short trips and anyone who hates a long transfer. You can be poolside within minutes of landing, which matters if you are arriving late or only staying a few nights.

The water here is sheltered and good for swimming, and you are close to Long Bay on the east coast and the dive and snorkel sites of the North Sound Marine Park. It is a quieter, more residential feel than Dickenson Bay, well suited to couples and repeat visitors who already know the island and want minimal fuss.

Adults-only vs family: how to choose

Most Antigua all-inclusives declare themselves clearly as either adults-only or family-friendly, and it is the single biggest filter to apply before you look at anything else.

Adults-only resorts

  • Found right around the island: on the Five Islands bays, on the Dickenson Bay strip, along the quiet east coast near Long Bay, and in the grown-up south around English Harbour.
  • Quieter pools, more romantic dining, and a calmer beach scene. Ideal for honeymoons, anniversaries, and couples who want adult company.
  • Often pair well with grown-up activities like yacht charters, scuba diving, and the Shirley Heights Sunday party.

Family-friendly resorts

  • Spread around the island rather than concentrated in one area. The calm water and wide beaches of Dickenson Bay and Jolly Harbour suit kids, but two of the biggest all-ages properties sit on Five Islands and the east coast, and several west and northwest resorts are adults-only or set a minimum age (Jolly Beach, for one, takes guests aged 12 and over). Check the age policy on the resort's own site before you book.
  • Kids' clubs, shallow swimming areas, and easy-access watersports. Look for gentle, reef-protected bays rather than open surf.
  • Family bases make day trips simple: a catamaran cruise, snorkeling, the rainforest zipline, or a visit to Stingray City all work for mixed ages.

If you are traveling with extended family or want flexibility, the village setup at Jolly Harbour gives you self-catering and restaurant options alongside resort meals.

What "all-inclusive" actually includes in Antigua

Coverage varies by property, but here is what is typical on the island and what to confirm before you book.

Usually included

  • All meals, often across several restaurants, plus snacks and room service at higher tiers.
  • Unlimited drinks, including local Wadadli beer and rum-based cocktails. Premium and top-shelf spirits, like aged English Harbour rum, are sometimes an upgrade.
  • Non-motorized watersports such as kayaks, paddleboards, and snorkel gear, plus pools, beach loungers, and basic entertainment.
  • Tips and government tax at most fully inclusive resorts (always confirm, as a service charge and tourism tax can be added).

Usually extra

  • Motorized watersports, scuba diving, and deep-sea fishing trips.
  • Off-site excursions like a Barbuda day trip, an island jeep safari, or a helicopter tour.
  • Spa treatments, premium dining venues, and sometimes lobster or specialty nights.

Prices on the island are quoted in East Caribbean dollars (EC$, roughly EC$2.70 to US$1), though US dollars are widely accepted and most resorts bill in US dollars. For excursions and tips outside the resort, carry some cash. See our local tips for the practical details, and review travel insurance before you go, especially in hurricane season from June to November.

Timing your all-inclusive trip

High season runs from mid-December to mid-April, when the weather is at its driest and sunniest and resort rates are highest. The shoulder months on either side often deliver near-identical weather for less money. The June-to-November hurricane season brings the lowest prices and a small storm risk, with September and October the quietest. If you want events, the south buzzes during Antigua Sailing Week in late April, and the island-wide Carnival peaks in late July into early August. Check current conditions on our Antigua weather page and the entry rules under visa requirements as you plan.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which area of Antigua is best for an all-inclusive resort?

It depends on your trip. Dickenson Bay in the northwest is the easiest all-rounder, with a calm beach, lots of resorts, and quick access to town and day trips. Jolly Harbour on the west coast adds village convenience and long swimming beaches, while English Harbour in the south suits couples who want history, sailing, and great restaurants.

Are Antigua all-inclusive resorts good for families?

Yes. Family-friendly resorts are spread around the island: Dickenson Bay and Jolly Harbour have calm water and wide beaches, while some of the largest all-ages properties are on Five Islands and the east coast. Look specifically for resorts that advertise a kids' club and shallow swimming areas, since some Antigua properties are adults-only.

What does all-inclusive include in Antigua?

Typically all meals, unlimited local drinks including Wadadli beer and cocktails, non-motorized watersports, pools, and entertainment. Motorized watersports, scuba diving, spa treatments, and off-site excursions like a Barbuda day trip are usually extra. Always confirm whether premium spirits, tips, and tourism tax are included.

Where are the adults-only all-inclusive resorts in Antigua?

Adults-only properties are scattered around the island: the Five Islands bays such as Galley Bay, the Dickenson Bay strip, the east coast near Long Bay, and the grown-up south around English Harbour. These areas tend to have quieter pools and more romantic dining, which suits honeymoons and couples' getaways.

Do I need a rental car if I stay at an all-inclusive in Antigua?

Not necessarily. The island is small enough that taxis and resort transfers cover most needs, and many guests rely on excursion pickups. A rental car is worth it if you want to beach-hop independently or explore the south and interior, but remember you drive on the left. See our transportation guide for details.

When is the cheapest time to book an all-inclusive in Antigua?

The lowest rates fall during the June-to-November hurricane season, especially September and October, when storm risk is highest but crowds are thinnest. The shoulder weeks just before mid-December and just after mid-April often pair near-peak weather with lower prices. Check our weather guide before committing to off-season dates.
guides.bestTime: Mid-December to mid-April for the driest weather; shoulder weeks for value
guides.budget: Varies widely by resort tier and season

guides.title: Antigua Cruise Port Guide for St. John's
guides.summary: Antigua cruise port sits on the St. John's waterfront, a 5-minute walk into town, with a day plan for Nelson's Dockyard, Shirley Heights, and a beach.
guides.html:
When your ship ties up in St. John's, you step off almost directly into the capital. The piers sit at the edge of downtown, so within a five-minute walk you are among duty-free shops, rum bars, and Georgian warehouses. Antigua Cruise Port lists five berths across three piers (the New Cruise Pier, the Heritage Quay Pier and the Nevis Street Pier), with extra ships tendering in from the deep-water harbor, so on a busy day the waterfront fills quickly. Redcliffe Quay, a short stroll south, is a shopping and dining quarter rather than a berth. The real decision is how far to roam: stay in town, chase one of the island's 365 beaches, or commit to the half-island run down to historic English Harbour. This guide maps each option against the clock so you make the call back to the gangway with time to spare.

Where You Dock: Heritage Quay and Redcliffe Quay

Most large ships berth at Heritage Quay, the modern shopping complex built for cruise traffic. It is a 5-minute walk from the gangway to the heart of St. John's, the capital and your launch pad for the day. Heritage Quay itself is wall-to-wall duty-free: jewelry, watches, liquor, perfume, and local crafts, plus a few bars where you can grab a Wadadli beer the moment you are ashore.

Redcliffe Quay, a short stroll south, has more character. Its restored 18th-century stone warehouses, once tied to the sugar and slave trades, now hold boutiques, galleries, and cafes shaded by sea-grape trees. If you only have an hour and want a sense of old Antigua without leaving the port zone, walk Redcliffe Quay and circle back through the public market.

What You Can Reach on Foot from the Pier

  • St. John's Cathedral, the twin-towered Baroque landmark on the hill, roughly a 10-minute uphill walk.
  • Museum of Antigua and Barbuda, housed in the old courthouse, a compact stop for island history.
  • Fort James and Fort James Beach, guarding the harbor mouth, a short taxi or a long walk northwest.
  • The vendors market and the food stalls around the public market, busiest on Friday and Saturday mornings.

Planning Your Hours: How Far Should You Go?

Cruise calls in St. John's typically run an all-aboard somewhere in the late afternoon, which leaves most passengers six to eight hours ashore. Match your ambition to that window. As a rule, build in a 60-to-90-minute buffer before all-aboard, because a single slow taxi or a busy beach bar tab can eat your cushion fast.

  • 2 to 3 hours: Stay in town. Walk Redcliffe Quay, the cathedral, and the market, then shop Heritage Quay.
  • 4 to 5 hours: Add a nearby beach (Dickenson Bay Beach, Fort James Beach, or Runaway Bay Beach) or a Stingray City tour.
  • 6+ hours: Commit to the south: Nelson's Dockyard, Shirley Heights, and a swim at Galleon Beach before heading back.

The Half-Island Highlight: Nelson's Dockyard and Shirley Heights

If you do one big thing from the port, make it English Harbour. English Harbour sits on the south coast, about 45 minutes by taxi from the St. John's pier across the island's interior. The Antigua and Barbuda Transport Board's official tariff sets the St. John's to Dockyard transfer at US$24, and that is per taxi for up to four passengers, with a small surcharge for each extra rider rather than a per-head fare. A guided tour that adds Clarence House, Shirley Heights or Fig Tree Drive is priced separately and costs considerably more, so confirm which you are buying, and in which currency, before you climb in. Antiguan taxis are unmetered and use government-set rates; share with other cruisers to cut the cost.

Nelson's Dockyard

Nelson's Dockyard is a restored dockyard and the centerpiece of Nelson's Dockyard National Park, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016. You can wander the restored sail loft, the officers' quarters, and the boat-builders' workshops, all still ringed by superyachts that moor here as they did in Lord Nelson's day. Allow about 60 to 90 minutes for the dockyard and its small museum, longer if you stop for lunch at one of the harborside cafes.

Shirley Heights

Above the dockyard, Shirley Heights is a restored 18th-century gun battery turned lookout, and the postcard view of Antigua: English Harbour and Falmouth Harbour stacked below you, yachts threading the channels. It is about a 5-minute taxi from the dockyard up the hill. If your ship happens to be in port on a Sunday afternoon, the legendary Shirley Heights Sunday party brings steel-pan and reggae bands, barbecue, and rum punch, though it typically peaks after most ships have sailed, so check your all-aboard time carefully.

Squeeze in a Beach

Down at the harbor, Galleon Beach and Pigeon Point Beach are short hops from the dockyard for a quick swim. On the way back to town you can detour to Ffryes Beach or Darkwood Beach along the southwest coast, two of the island's easiest sand-and-bar combinations.

Closer to Port: Beaches and Stingrays

If a full half-island run feels tight, plenty of payoff sits within 15 to 30 minutes of the pier.

  • Dickenson Bay to the north has the island's most developed beach strip: calm water, sunbeds, watersports, and beach bars at Dickenson Bay Beach, roughly a 15-minute taxi from the port.
  • Stingray City takes you to a shallow sandbar offshore where you can stand waist-deep and feed southern stingrays. Boats leave from the land base in Seatons on the north-east coast, and the round trip fits a cruise day with margin to spare.
  • Five Islands, just west of town, holds quieter sands like Galley Bay Beach and Deep Bay Beach, the latter with a snorkelable shipwreck close to shore.
  • Snorkelers and divers can book a snorkeling trip or catamaran day cruise, but check the run time against all-aboard, as full-day catamarans rarely return before late afternoon.

Getting Around from the Cruise Port

Taxis

Taxis line up right outside Heritage Quay. Antigua drives on the left, and taxis are unmetered with fixed government rates, so always agree the price in US dollars or EC dollars before departing. Hourly hire (a private driver who waits while you explore) is a smart move for the dockyard run, often around US$24 per hour with a two-hour minimum, plus waiting time. The East Caribbean dollar trades near EC$2.70 to US$1, and US dollars are widely accepted, though you may get change in EC.

Tours Booked Ahead

For first-time cruisers, an excursion booked through the cruise line takes the pressure off: lines such as Royal Caribbean state that the ship will wait if one of their own tours runs late. An independently booked tour carries no such guarantee, and getting back before all-aboard stays your responsibility, so ask the operator in writing what happens if the tour overruns. Popular choices include the island jeep safari, the rainforest zipline near Wallings Nature Reserve, and a guided catamaran cruise down the coast.

Buses and Self-Drive

Local buses leave from the West Bus Station, a few blocks from the port, and run cheaply toward English Harbour, but service is informal and slow, and they stop running early, so they are risky on a fixed sailing schedule. Renting a car for a single port day is rarely worth the paperwork and the local driving permit, though our transportation guide covers the full picture if you want it.

Eat and Drink Like You Mean It

Do not leave without tasting the island. Order fungie and pepperpot, Antigua's national dish, or Antiguan saltfish with ducana at a market stall or a Redcliffe Quay cafe. Wash it down with a cold Wadadli beer or an English Harbour rum, both made on island. If the famous Antigua black pineapple is in season, the market is the place to try it. Our cuisine overview rounds out what to look for.

Quick Cruise-Day Checklist

  • Confirm your exact all-aboard time the moment you step off, and set a phone alarm 90 minutes ahead.
  • Carry small US bills for taxis, plus a little for tips and the market.
  • Pack reef-safe sunscreen, water, and a hat: Antigua is warm, dry, and sunny most of the year.
  • Agree every taxi fare before you ride, and ask the driver to wait for the return if you go to the dockyard.
  • For weather and seasonal timing, check our Antigua weather guide before you book anything outdoors.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where do cruise ships dock in Antigua?

Ships dock on the St. John's waterfront at the edge of downtown. Antigua Cruise Port lists five berths, across the New Cruise Pier, the Heritage Quay Pier and the Nevis Street Pier, with extra ships tendering passengers in from the deep-water harbor. Heritage Quay is a shopping complex about five minutes' walk from the heart of the capital; Redcliffe Quay nearby is a shopping area, not a berth. Check which pier your ship is assigned to.

Can you walk to anything from the Antigua cruise port?

Yes. St. John's is very walkable from the pier. Within 10 minutes on foot you can reach St. John's Cathedral, Redcliffe Quay's historic warehouses, the public market, and the Museum of Antigua and Barbuda. For beaches and Nelson's Dockyard you will need a taxi or tour.

How do you get from the cruise port to Nelson's Dockyard?

Take a taxi from outside Heritage Quay. The drive to English Harbour and Nelson's Dockyard takes about 45 minutes across the island, and the Transport Board's official one-way tariff is US$24 per taxi for up to four passengers, though pier drivers often quote more, so agree the fare first. Agree the price before departing, and consider hourly hire so the driver waits and brings you back.

Is one day enough to see Antigua from a cruise?

One day lets you do one major thing well, not everything. With six to eight hours ashore you can pair Nelson's Dockyard and Shirley Heights with a short beach stop, or spend the day at a nearby beach like Dickenson Bay plus shopping in town. Trying to combine the dockyard, a far beach, and a long catamaran cruise in a single call is too tight.

What is the best beach near the Antigua cruise port?

Dickenson Bay Beach to the north is the easiest, about 15 minutes by taxi, with calm water, sunbeds, and beach bars. Fort James Beach and Runaway Bay Beach are even closer. For fewer crowds, Deep Bay or Galley Bay in the Five Islands area are short rides west of town.

Do I need cash in Antigua for a cruise day?

Carry some. Antigua uses the East Caribbean dollar (about EC$2.70 to US$1), but US dollars are widely accepted for taxis, tours, and most shops. Bring small US bills for fares and tips, and expect any change to come back in EC dollars. Cards work in larger stores and restaurants but not always at market stalls or with taxi drivers.
guides.bestTime: High season runs mid-December to mid-April; any clear day works for a port call, but Sunday lets you catch the Shirley Heights party if your sailing allows.
guides.duration: Day trip from the cruise port (typically 6 to 8 hours ashore)
guides.budget: Port shopping is free to browse; the official Transport Board tariff lists St. John's to the Dockyard at US$24 one way per taxi (up to four people); pier drivers often quote more, so agree the fare first.

guides.title: Antigua Travel Guide for First-Timers
guides.summary: Antigua travel guide for first-timers covers V.C. Bird Airport arrival, EC dollars, left-side driving, where to stay, and the best months to visit.
guides.html:
Antigua and Barbuda is a two-island nation in the Eastern Caribbean, roughly 1,300 miles southeast of Miami and a short hop from islands like St. Kitts, Guadeloupe, and St. Martin. The country is small enough to circle by car in an afternoon, yet it packs in 365 beaches, a UNESCO-listed Georgian dockyard, and a sailing culture that draws crews from around the world. This guide walks first-time visitors through the practical decisions: how to arrive, how to move around, what to do with your money, where to base yourself, and what to actually do once you are there.

Where Antigua Is and How to Get There

Visitors arriving by air fly into V.C. Bird International Airport (airport code ANU), on the northeast corner of the main island, about 8 km (5 miles) from the capital, St. John's. The smaller sister island, Barbuda, sits about 30 miles north and is reached by a short domestic flight or a ferry.

Direct flights

  • From the US: American flies year-round from Miami and New York (JFK), with seasonal service from Charlotte, Atlanta, and elsewhere in the winter high season.
  • From the UK and Europe: British Airways and Virgin Atlantic connect London to Antigua, with a flight time of around 8 to 9 hours.
  • From Canada: year-round service runs from Toronto, with additional seasonal flights.

Most US east-coast flights take roughly 4 hours. Once you land, immigration is straightforward for short visits; check our visa requirements page for your nationality before you book, and read the practical airport guide for arrivals, taxis, and SIM cards.

Getting Around the Island

Antigua drives on the left, a British holdover, with right-hand-drive cars. Roads are generally fine on main routes and rougher on rural lanes, and signage can be thin, so a phone map helps. Our transportation guide covers every option in detail.

Renting a car

A rental car gives you the freedom to chase beaches and reach inland sights like Fig Tree Drive and Betty's Hope on your own schedule. Visitors need a local driving permit, which costs roughly EC$50 (about US$20); rental agencies almost always arrange it for you at pickup, so bring your home license. Drive cautiously on your first day until the left-side habit sets in, and watch for free-roaming goats on country roads.

Taxis and tours

Taxis are unmetered with government-set rates, so agree the fare before you set off and confirm whether the quote is in EC or US dollars. For visitors who would rather not drive, a half-day taxi tour or an island jeep safari covers the headline sights without the wheel. There is no comprehensive public bus network aimed at tourists, though local buses run between St. John's and some villages for very little.

Money, Costs, and Practical Basics

The local currency is the East Caribbean dollar (EC$), pegged at about EC$2.70 to one US dollar. US dollars are widely accepted, but you will often get change in EC, and paying in local currency usually works out slightly better. Cards are accepted at hotels, larger restaurants, and tour operators; carry some cash for beach bars, taxis, and small vendors.

  • Language: English is the official language, so there is no barrier for most visitors.
  • Tipping: many restaurants add a service charge; if not, 10 to 15 percent is standard.
  • Power and plugs: outlets are commonly 110V, US-style, though some hotels also fit 220V, so a universal adapter is wise.
  • Safety: Antigua is generally relaxed; use ordinary common sense and check our local tips and emergency contacts before you travel.

Travel insurance is worth arranging given the cost of medical care abroad and the chance of a weather disruption in hurricane season; see our travel insurance guide for what to look for.

Where to Stay by Area

Antigua has no single resort strip. Instead, distinct areas suit different trips, and your choice shapes the whole holiday.

Dickenson Bay and the northwest

Dickenson Bay is the classic first-timer base: a long calm stretch of sand with watersports, beach bars, and easy access to St. John's. Dickenson Bay Beach and nearby Runaway Bay are made for swimming and sunset cocktails.

English Harbour and the south

English Harbour is the historic and sailing heart of the island, home to Nelson's Dockyard and the famous Shirley Heights lookout. It suits visitors who want character, restaurants, and yacht-watching, with beaches like Galleon Beach and Pigeon Point close by.

Jolly Harbour and the west coast

Jolly Harbour and the Five Islands area offer marina life, golf, and a run of excellent west-facing beaches, including Jolly Beach, Valley Church, Ffryes, and Darkwood, all known for calm water and big sunsets.

Long Bay and the east

Long Bay on the Atlantic side is quieter and reef-sheltered, with Long Bay Beach ideal for families and snorkeling straight off the sand.

Barbuda

Barbuda is for travelers chasing emptiness and the famous pink-sand beach. It works as a day trip or an overnight escape; see our Barbuda day trip for how to plan it.

Top Things to Do on a First Visit

You will not run out of options. A strong first-timer mix blends history, water, and one or two splurges.

  • History and views: tour Nelson's Dockyard, the UNESCO-listed Georgian naval yard, then catch the Sunday-evening Shirley Heights party for steel drums, barbecue, and a sweeping harbor sunset.
  • On the water: a catamaran day cruise or a private sailing charter shows off the coastline; snorkeling, scuba diving, and the popular Stingray City tour get you under the surface.
  • Inland adventure: the rainforest zipline and Wallings Nature Reserve add some green to a beach trip, while Devil's Bridge and Fig Tree Drive reward a self-drive day.
  • Capital and culture: wander St. John's, see St. John's Cathedral, and browse the Museum of Antigua and Barbuda.
  • Eat local: try the national dish fungie and pepperpot, sweet Antigua Black pineapple, and a cold Wadadli beer. Our cuisine overview rounds up what to order.

When to Go

Antigua is warm, sunny, and breezy for most of the year. The peak season runs from mid-December to mid-April, with the most reliable weather and the highest prices. Hurricane season spans June to November, with the greatest risk from August to October; storms are uncommon on any given day but worth planning around. Check our Antigua weather guide for a month-by-month breakdown.

The calendar also shapes the experience. Sailing fans aim for Antigua Sailing Week in late April (April 21–25 in 2027) or the Classic Yacht Regatta just before it. Antigua Carnival lights up late July into early August with music, costumes, and street parties. For the calmest swimming and the best snorkeling visibility, the drier winter and spring months are hard to beat.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days do you need in Antigua for a first visit?

Five to seven days is a comfortable first trip. That gives you time for a couple of beach days, a catamaran or sailing cruise, the Nelson's Dockyard and Shirley Heights combination, and a self-drive day inland, without rushing. Add two or three more days if you want a Barbuda overnight or a slower, beach-focused pace.

Do I need a car in Antigua, or can I get by without one?

You can manage without a car if you stay at a resort and use taxis and tours, which many first-timers do. A rental gives you far more freedom to reach quieter beaches and inland sights on your own schedule, but remember you drive on the left and need a local permit, which rental agencies arrange. If you are nervous about left-side driving, mix taxis with one or two guided tours instead.

What currency should I bring to Antigua?

The local currency is the East Caribbean dollar, pegged at about EC$2.70 to one US dollar, and US dollars are widely accepted. Cards work at hotels, larger restaurants, and tour operators, but carry cash for taxis, beach bars, and small vendors. Paying in EC dollars often gives slightly better value than paying in US dollars.

Is Antigua safe for tourists?

Antigua is generally a relaxed and safe destination for visitors who use ordinary common sense: secure your valuables, avoid isolated areas late at night, and watch your belongings on the beach. Review our local tips and emergency contacts pages before you travel so you know who to call and what to expect. Most trips pass without any trouble at all.

When is the best time to visit Antigua?

Mid-December to mid-April brings the most reliable sunshine and the liveliest events, but it is also the priciest and busiest period. June to November is hurricane season, cheaper and quieter, with the highest storm risk from August to October. For warm water, calm seas, and good value just outside peak, late April, May, and early December are sweet spots.

Do US and UK visitors need a visa for Antigua?

Citizens of the US, UK, Canada, and the EU typically do not need a visa for short tourist stays, but you must meet the passport-validity requirements for your nationality and must be able to show an onward or return ticket. Entry rules change, so confirm the current requirements for your nationality on our visa requirements page before you book. If in doubt, check your government's official travel advice as well.
guides.bestTime: Mid-December to mid-April for the most reliable sunshine; late April to May for events and better value.
guides.duration: 5 to 7 days for a first visit
guides.budget: Mid-range; US dollars accepted, EC$ for small vendors and taxis.

guides.title: Antigua Honeymoon Guide: Romance & Beaches
guides.summary: Antigua honeymoon planning covers 365 beaches, quiet versus lively bases, sunset spots, private sailing, Shirley Heights, and a two-island Barbuda day trip.
guides.html:
Antigua was built for couples. The island claims 365 beaches, one for every day of the year, which means you can spend a two-week honeymoon and never lay your towel on the same sand twice. Add calm Caribbean water, a sailing heritage that fills English Harbour with yachts at sunset, and a string of adults-only resorts on their own private coves, and you have one of the easier islands in the Caribbean to plan a romantic trip around. This guide covers where to base yourselves, the beaches worth the drive, the best places to watch the sun go down, and the couple experiences that justify the splurge.

Choosing your base: quiet or lively

Antigua is small (you can drive coast to coast in under an hour), so wherever you stay you can reach the whole island. But the mood changes a lot by area, and that is the first decision to make as a couple.

Lively and social

  • Dickenson Bay on the northwest coast is the island's busiest beach strip: water-sports operators, beach bars, and the long calm sweep of Dickenson Bay Beach. Good if you want company, easy dining, and sunset cocktails without a taxi ride.
  • Jolly Harbour on the west coast is a marina village with restaurants, a golf course, and the broad sands of Jolly Beach next door. A relaxed base with self-catering options and an easy walk to dinner.
  • St. John's, the capital, suits couples who want to be near shops, the St. John's Cathedral, and the Museum of Antigua and Barbuda, with the rest of the island a short drive away.

Quiet and secluded

  • English Harbour in the south is the most atmospheric base on the island: a yachting town wrapped around the UNESCO-listed Nelson's Dockyard, with quiet swimming at Galleon Beach and Pigeon Point Beach, and Shirley Heights on the hill above.
  • Five Islands, a peninsula west of the capital, holds the calm, palm-backed Galley Bay Beach and Hawksbill Beach, both away from the crowds.
  • Long Bay on the quiet east coast has a reef close to shore and the gentle, shallow water of Long Bay Beach, good for couples who want to swim and snorkel straight off the sand.
  • Barbuda, the sister island, is the ultimate escape: a handful of rooms, frigate birds, and miles of empty pink-tinged sand. More on the day trip below.

The most romantic beaches

With 365 to choose from, the trick is matching the beach to the moment. Here are the ones couples come back for.

  • Sunset swims: Ffryes Beach and the neighbouring Valley Church Beach on the west coast both face the setting sun, with bright water and a beach bar each for an evening drink.
  • Postcard calm: Darkwood Beach, also west-facing, is a long quiet curve with views toward Montserrat on a clear day.
  • Worth the drive: Half Moon Bay Beach on the far southeast is a crescent of sand backed by sea grape, wilder and less developed than the west coast, with a calmer protected end for swimming.
  • Hideaway feel: Rendezvous Bay Beach is reachable on foot, by boat, or by four-wheel drive, which keeps it close to empty even in high season.
  • Easy and pretty: Deep Bay Beach shelters a shipwreck snorkellers love and the ruins of Fort Barrington on the headland above. Carlisle Bay Beach and Morris Bay Beach in the south are calm, palm-lined, and quiet.
  • The pink one: Pink Sand Beach on Barbuda is the headline act, an 11-mile stretch where crushed shell tints the sand soft pink. Best seen on a day trip (below).

For a wider shortlist by mood and location, browse the full beach directory, including family-friendly Runaway Bay Beach and the lively Fort James Beach near the capital.

Where to watch the sunset

Antigua's south and west coasts face the sunset, so you are spoiled for choice. A few spots stand out for couples.

Shirley Heights

Shirley Heights is the classic. The old military lookout sits high above English Harbour, and the view down over the yachts to the open Caribbean is the most photographed scene on the island. On Sundays the Shirley Heights Sunday party brings live steel pan and reggae, a barbecue, and a crowd, the most fun way to end a honeymoon week. For something quieter, check the event schedule before visiting: Thursday also hosts barbecue parties. The hilltop sits inside Nelson's Dockyard National Park.

West-coast beach bars

If you would rather have your feet in the sand, the bars at Ffryes Beach, Darkwood Beach, and Turners Beach all line up the sun over the water with a rum punch in hand. Time a catamaran day cruise to finish near golden hour and you watch the sky change from the deck.

Couple experiences worth booking

Beaches and resorts make the trip easy, but the experiences below are what couples remember.

Get out on the water

  • Private sailing. Antigua is the sailing capital of the Caribbean, so a private yacht charter is the signature splurge: just the two of you, a skipper, and a secluded cove for lunch and a swim. A shared catamaran day cruise is the relaxed, lower-cost version, often circling to Barbuda or along the coast.
  • Snorkel and dive together. The reefs are close to shore. Book a snorkelling trip, go further out on a scuba dive, or float with the rays on the Stingray City tour at Stingray City.
  • Paddle at dawn. A quiet paddleboard or kayak session in a sheltered bay is a calm way to start a honeymoon morning before the resort wakes up.

See the island from above

  • A helicopter tour over the coastline and out toward Montserrat's volcano is the once-in-a-trip thrill, and the aerial view of all those beaches is unforgettable.
  • Land-based romance: a horseback ride along the sand, the treetop rainforest zipline, or a slow drive down Fig Tree Drive through the rainforest to the south coast.

History and a quieter day out

Wander the restored Georgian buildings of Nelson's Dockyard, walk to the windmills of Betty's Hope, or watch the Atlantic surge through Devil's Bridge on the wild east coast. For a green half-day, Wallings Nature Reserve has shaded trails and a reservoir.

A Barbuda day trip for two

If you want one truly off-grid day, take the Barbuda day trip. The sister island is reached by a short ferry or a quick flight, and most of it is empty: 11 miles of pink-tinged sand at Pink Sand Beach, the Codrington Lagoon, and one of the largest frigate bird colonies in the world at the frigate bird sanctuary. Bring water and reef-safe sunscreen, because services are sparse. It is the closest thing to having a Caribbean island to yourselves.

When to go and how to plan

The driest, sunniest stretch runs from mid-December to mid-April, which is also high season, so book well ahead for honeymoon dates. May, June, and late November sit in the shoulder season with good weather, fewer crowds, and lower rates. The official Atlantic hurricane season runs June to November, with the highest risk usually August to October, so travel insurance is worth it if you go then. Check current conditions on the Antigua weather page before you pack.

A few practical notes for couples:

  • Antigua drives on the left. If you plan to explore beyond your resort, see the transportation guide for car hire, taxis, and the local driving permit.
  • Check entry rules early on the visa requirements page, and consider travel insurance for the hurricane months.
  • For etiquette, tipping, and money tips (the East Caribbean dollar is the local currency, US dollars are widely accepted), read the local tips.
  • You will land at V.C. Bird International Airport, a short drive from most resorts. Save the emergency contacts page to your phone just in case.

To toast the trip the local way, share an Antigua Black pineapple at breakfast, sip English Harbour rum at sunset, and clink a cold Wadadli on the beach. See the full Antigua cuisine guide for more.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time for an Antigua honeymoon?

Mid-December to mid-April is the driest, sunniest, and most reliable window, though it is also the busiest and priciest, so book early. May, June, and late November offer warm weather, thinner crowds, and lower rates. Avoid the peak hurricane months of August to October unless you take out travel insurance and stay flexible.

Which part of Antigua is best for a honeymoon?

For seclusion and atmosphere, base yourselves in the south around English Harbour, near Nelson's Dockyard and Shirley Heights, or on the quiet Five Islands peninsula. For an easy, social trip with bars and water sports on your doorstep, choose Dickenson Bay or Jolly Harbour on the west coast. The island is small, so you can stay in one spot and still reach every beach.

What are the most romantic beaches in Antigua?

For sunset swims, head to west-facing Ffryes Beach, Valley Church Beach, or Darkwood Beach. For a quieter, wilder feel, try Half Moon Bay on the southeast coast or hike or boat in to Rendezvous Bay. The standout is Pink Sand Beach on Barbuda, an 11-mile stretch best reached on a day trip.

What is the most romantic thing to do in Antigua as a couple?

A private yacht charter is the signature Antigua experience, since the island is the Caribbean's sailing capital. Pair it with sunset drinks at Shirley Heights, which looks down over English Harbour, and consider a helicopter tour for the aerial view of all those beaches. A Barbuda day trip gives you a near-empty island for a day.

Is Antigua good for couples who want to avoid crowds?

Yes. While Dickenson Bay and Jolly Harbour are busier, the south coast around English Harbour, the Five Islands peninsula, and the east coast at Long Bay stay quiet. Beaches like Rendezvous Bay and Half Moon Bay are hard to reach and rarely crowded, and a day trip to Barbuda is about as secluded as the Caribbean gets.

How long should we stay in Antigua for a honeymoon?

Seven to ten nights is the sweet spot: enough time to settle into a resort, sample several beaches, take a sailing trip, and add a Barbuda day or a helicopter tour without rushing. Five nights works for a shorter break, while two weeks lets you split your stay between a lively base and a quiet one.
guides.bestTime: Mid-December to mid-April for the driest, sunniest weather; May, June, and late November for fewer crowds and lower rates.
