facts.value: Informal roadside parking near the beach

beaches.name: Carlisle Bay
beaches.tagline: Palm-fringed crescent framed by green hills
beaches.summary: A long, palm-fringed crescent on the south coast at Old Road, framed by green hills and a luxury resort. Calm, protected water, good snorkeling, and a serene, upscale feel.
beaches.html:
Carlisle Bay arcs along the base of a deep, sheltered bay on Antigua's south coast, near the village of Old Road. A roughly one-kilometre crescent of pale sand is backed by a dense fringe of coconut palms and framed by steep green hills, giving it a serene, almost secluded character. The bay's protected shape keeps the water calm and clear.

An intricate reef system in and around the bay makes for good snorkeling, with a variety of tropical fish in the clear shallows. The acclaimed Carlisle Bay resort fronts the beach, lending the area a quiet, upscale atmosphere, but as on every Antiguan beach the sand and water are public and open to all.

This is one of the more tranquil south-coast beaches, well suited to relaxed swimming, snorkeling, and long walks beneath the palms. Public facilities are limited outside the resort, so bring water and supplies. The combination of calm water, abundant palm shade, reef life, and a beautiful hill-framed setting makes Carlisle Bay a standout on the south coast.

Reaching the beach involves a drive to Old Road on the south coast, and public parking is limited, so come earlier in the day. There is no lifeguard, but the sheltered bay keeps the water calm. Carlisle Bay pairs well with a visit to nearby Morris Bay just to the west, or with the historic sites around English Harbour a little further east. Snorkelers should bring their own gear to make the most of the reef. For travelers who value shade, calm water, and a peaceful, scenic setting over bars and bustle, Carlisle Bay is one of the most restful beaches on the island.

photo.alt: Carlisle Bay beach at Old Road, Antigua

beaches.name: Coco Point Beach
beaches.tagline: Barbuda's secluded southern tip where two coasts meet
beaches.summary: A remote, pink-tinged white sand beach at the southern tip of Barbuda, where the calm leeward coast meets the breezier windward side beside the former K Club estate.
beaches.html:
Coco Point sits at the far south of Barbuda, the slender tip where the island's calm leeward coast and its breezier windward coast finally meet. The sand here is the pale, pink-tinged white that Barbuda is famous for, the colour drawn from crushed coral and tiny shell fragments worked into the shore over centuries. It is a long, quiet stretch with private residences and resort amenities behind it, now part of the private Barbuda Ocean Club estate.

The appeal of Coco Point is its remoteness. Nobu offers beachside dining and drinks on Princess Diana Beach. On the leeward, west-facing side the water is glassy and shallow, ideal for slow swims and long barefoot walks. Round towards the windward side and you feel the open Atlantic, with a little more swell and breeze. Like all beaches in Antigua and Barbuda, the sand is public by law, though the land behind much of it is private.

Getting here takes intent. Barbuda is reached by ferry from Jolly Harbour Marina or a short flight from Antigua, and Coco Point lies at the southern end of the island, well beyond the main settlement. Most visitors come on a guided Barbuda day trip, often paired with the pink-sand beaches further north and the famous frigate bird colony in the lagoon.

Come prepared for a wild, unserviced shore. Bring water and sun protection; Nobu offers paid cabanas, showers and changing rooms on Princess Diana Beach. Reef shoes are useful where the sand gives way to coral, and on the windward side currents can strengthen, so weaker swimmers should favour the sheltered leeward water. Earlier in the day usually brings the lightest wind and the calmest sea.

photo.alt: Princess Diana Beach at Coco Point, Barbuda

beaches.name: Darkwood Beach
beaches.tagline: Roadside beach with Montserrat views
beaches.summary: A scenic roadside beach on the southwest coast with calm, clear water and views across to Montserrat. A local favorite for its beach bar, easy access, and reliable snorkeling.
beaches.html:
Darkwood Beach is an easygoing stretch of pale sand on the southwest coast south of Jolly Harbour, right beside the coast road. Its accessibility is part of the appeal: you can pull off the road, walk a few steps onto the sand, and be swimming in calm, clear Caribbean water within minutes.

The water here is sheltered and usually gentle, with rocky patches and seagrass that make for decent snorkeling close to shore. On clear days you can see the volcanic island of Montserrat on the horizon to the southwest. A long-running beach bar serves cold drinks and fresh seafood, giving the beach a relaxed, local atmosphere.

Darkwood is popular with both visitors and Antiguans, especially at weekends, but it rarely feels crowded. Natural shade is limited, so an umbrella helps, and the parking is simply the roadside. The combination of calm water, easy access, Montserrat views, and a friendly bar makes it one of the most reliable beach stops on the southwest coast.

Because it sits right on the main coast road, Darkwood is a natural stop on a self-drive day exploring the southwest, easily combined with Turner's Beach just to the south or Ffryes Beach to the north. There is no lifeguard, but the sheltered water is usually calm and good for swimming. Bring water shoes if you plan to snorkel, since there are rocky and seagrass patches close in. With nothing complicated about it, just park, swim, snorkel, and grab lunch at the bar, Darkwood is the kind of easy, scenic beach you end up returning to.

beaches.name: Deep Bay
beaches.tagline: Horseshoe bay with a snorkelable shipwreck
beaches.summary: A sheltered, horseshoe-shaped bay on the Five Islands peninsula with a shipwreck resting in the middle of the bay, snorkelable from shore. Calm water, a hilltop fort, and a quiet, scenic setting.
beaches.html:
Deep Bay is a near-perfect horseshoe of calm, clear water tucked into the Five Islands peninsula west of St. John's. The bay is almost fully enclosed by land, so the water stays glassy and protected, ideal for swimming and easy snorkeling. The pale sand and green hills give it a quiet, postcard quality.

The bay's signature feature is the wreck of the Andes, a 19th-century sailing ship that sank here and now lies in shallow water in the middle of the bay. Its masts once broke the surface; today snorkelers swim out from the beach to explore the encrusted hull and the fish that shelter around it. It is one of the few shore-accessible wrecks on the island.

Above the northern headland sit the ruins of Fort Barrington, reached by a short uphill walk that rewards you with sweeping views over the bay and coastline. Deep Bay has few facilities and can be quiet outside of resort and tour visits, so bring water and shade. The calm, scenic water and the wreck make it a favorite for snorkelers and photographers.

The bay is reached by a short drive onto the Five Islands peninsula, and parking is limited, so arrive earlier in the day for the calmest water and the best snorkeling visibility. There is no lifeguard; check water conditions and boat activity before swimming. Combine a swim and a wreck snorkel with the hike up to Fort Barrington for a half-day that mixes beach, history, and panoramic views, all within easy reach of St. John's. For its size, Deep Bay packs in more variety than almost any other beach near the capital.

facts.label: Access
facts.value: Road may be rough; steps and a walk

beaches.name: Dickenson Bay
beaches.tagline: Antigua's famous calm-water resort beach
beaches.summary: Antigua's most famous beach: a long, gently curving arc of white sand on the calm northwest coast, lined with resorts, beach bars, and watersports. The island's liveliest and most developed stretch of shoreline.
beaches.html:
Dickenson Bay is the beach most visitors picture when they imagine Antigua. A broad, shallow crescent of soft white sand wraps around a sheltered bay on the leeward northwest coast, where the Caribbean stays calm and warm almost year round. Because it faces west, the water is glassy in the mornings and the sunsets here are some of the best on the island.

This is the most developed beach in Antigua, anchoring the Dickenson Bay resort strip just north of the capital, St. John's. Loungers, beach bars, restaurants, and watersports operators line the sand, so you can hire a paddleboard, book a snorkel trip, or settle in for rum punch and live music without leaving your towel. Hobie Cats and kayaks launch from the calm shallows.

The bay shelves gently, making it excellent for swimming and ideal for families with young children. Quieter, quainter Runaway Bay begins just to the south if you want the same calm water with fewer crowds. Dickenson Bay gets busy on cruise days and weekends, so come early to claim shade and enjoy the still morning water.

Practical notes: there is no dedicated lifeguard service, but the calm, shallow water keeps conditions forgiving, and watersports operators are on hand through the day. Natural shade is limited beyond the bars and a few sea-grape trees, so an umbrella helps in the middle of the day. The beach is an easy ten-minute drive from St. John's and the cruise terminal, which makes it a popular first stop. For the full experience, time a visit for late afternoon, settle in for a rum punch, and stay for the sunset over the water.

beaches.name: Dutchman's Bay
beaches.tagline: The airport-side beach for kitesurfers and windsurfers
beaches.summary: The quiet north-coast beach closest to the airport, just a few minutes from V.C. Bird International Airport. A shallow, breezy bay where kitesurfers and windsurfers ride the steady trade winds.
beaches.html:
Dutchman's Bay is the beach you can reach by car from V.C. Bird International Airport, just a few minutes from V.C. Bird International Airport. That alone makes it one of the handiest stretches of sand on Antigua's north coast: a quiet, breezy bay that works perfectly as a first taste of the island when you land, or a last swim before you fly home with your bags already packed.

The water here is shallow and warm, shelving out gently over a sandy bottom, while a steady trade-wind breeze ruffles the surface. Those conditions are exactly why the bay has become a favourite with kitesurfers and windsurfers, who rig up along the shore and use the flat, protected water to launch. It is a great place to watch the sails skim back and forth, and a friendly spot to take a lesson if you have been thinking about trying kitesurfing or windsurfing in Antigua.

Because it sits away from the resort strip, Dutchman's Bay stays low-key and uncrowded. There are few facilities, so bring water, snacks, and your own shade, and remember that like every beach in Antigua this one is public by law. The breeze that delights the sailors also keeps the sand cooler than the calmer leeward bays, which is welcome under the midday sun. Nearby Jabberwock Beach shares the same windy north-coast character if you want to chase the kites a little further along the coast.

Mornings tend to be quieter and the light is lovely, while afternoons usually bring the firmest, most reliable wind for sailing. Swimming is easy in the shallow water close to shore, though stronger gusts can push the surface around, so keep an eye on conditions and on any kites overhead. With the airport so close, Dutchman's Bay is the obvious choice when you want sand and sea bookending a flight rather than a long drive across the island.

beaches.name: Ffryes Beach
beaches.tagline: Postcard beach with a hilltop sunset bar
beaches.summary: A picture-perfect southwest-coast beach framed by green headlands, with soft white sand and calm turquoise water. A beloved sunset spot anchored by the lively Dennis's beach bar above the sand.
beaches.html:
Ffryes Beach (sometimes written Ffryes Bay) is one of the most beautiful beaches on Antigua's southwest coast, a clean curve of soft white sand framed by two green headlands. The calm, turquoise Caribbean water is excellent for swimming, and the scenic setting south of Jolly Harbour makes it a favorite for photos and lazy beach days.

On the bluff above the sand sits a long-established beach bar and restaurant with sweeping views over the bay, a popular spot for lunch, sunset drinks, and live music. The beach itself stays relaxed, with room to spread out even when the bar is busy. Loungers and umbrellas are usually available to rent.

Because the bay faces southwest, the water is calm and the sunsets are superb, drawing a small crowd most evenings. Just to the north lies equally lovely Valley Church Beach, so the two are easy to combine. Natural shade is limited, so claim a spot near the bar or bring an umbrella, and arrive in good time for sunset.

Parking is straightforward, with a small lot and roadside spaces, and there is no lifeguard, though the calm water makes for easy swimming. Ffryes is a short drive south of Jolly Harbour, which makes it a simple add-on to a southwest-coast beach day. Many visitors spend the afternoon on the sand, then move up to the bar for sunset drinks and dinner as the sky turns. Between its postcard looks, calm turquoise water, and the lively bar above, Ffryes manages to be both a serene swimming beach and a social sunset hangout, which is a rare combination on the island.

beaches.name: Fort James Beach
beaches.tagline: Local beach beneath an 18th-century fort
beaches.summary: The beach where locals go: a wide, shallow bay just outside St. John's, watched over by the ruins of an 18th-century fort. Calm water, weekend cookouts, and an authentic, unpolished vibe.
beaches.html:
Fort James Beach sits at the mouth of St. John's harbour, a short drive from the capital and cruise terminal. It takes its name from the 18th-century Fort James, whose weathered cannons and stone walls still guard the headland above the sand. The combination of an easy beach and a free historic site makes it a popular half-day outing.

This is one of Antigua's most local beaches. The bay is wide and shallow with calm, clear water, and at weekends Antiguan families gather here for cookouts, music, and easy swimming. A few beach bars serve cold drinks and fresh seafood, and the relaxed, unpolished atmosphere is a refreshing contrast to the resort strips.

The gentle shelving and sheltered water make Fort James good for children and casual swimmers. Shade is patchy, so bring an umbrella. Because it is so close to town, it can get busy on cruise days, but mornings are usually quiet. Pair a swim with a wander up to the fort for harbour views over the capital.

Take care when swimming; currents can be deceptively strong, and the easy parking and short drive from the cruise port make Fort James one of the simplest beach trips on the island. It pairs naturally with a morning of sightseeing in St. John's, and the free historic site adds a little context to a lazy afternoon. For travelers who want to see how Antiguans actually spend a beach day, with cookouts, music, and an unhurried, welcoming atmosphere, Fort James is one of the most genuine choices near the capital.

beaches.name: Galleon Beach
beaches.tagline: Turtle snorkeling at the mouth of English Harbour
beaches.summary: A tranquil beach in Freeman's Bay at the mouth of English Harbour, with calm water and a reef where hawksbill turtles are often seen. Walkable to Nelson's Dockyard and Shirley Heights.
beaches.html:
Galleon Beach lies in Freeman's Bay, right at the mouth of English Harbour on the south coast. This picturesque, tranquil beach has soft sand and calm, warm water, framed by green headlands and dotted with historic associations from Antigua's great age of sail. It is one of the most scenic and serene beaches in the area.

The reef just offshore is a highlight: snorkelers regularly spot green turtles grazing on the seagrass, along with reef fish and the occasional ray. The protected water is calm and clear, making it excellent for both swimming and easy snorkeling straight from the beach. Beach restaurants serve drinks and lunch in season; check whether they are open before visiting.

Galleon's position makes it a perfect pairing with the area's history. It is a short boat ride or a scenic walk from Nelson's Dockyard, and the famous sunset viewpoint at Shirley Heights looks down over this very stretch of coast. For a beach day steeped in setting and good snorkeling, Galleon is hard to top.

Many visitors reach Galleon by water taxi from the dockyard, which is the easiest option, since road access and parking are limited. There is no lifeguard, but the protected water in Freeman's Bay is calm and well suited to swimming and snorkeling. Bring your own mask and fins to make the most of the reef and the turtles, and an umbrella for shade. With its history, scenery, and reliable wildlife sightings all in one sheltered bay, Galleon is a standout for travelers exploring English Harbour who want their beach time to come with a story.

photo.alt: The bay beside Galleon Beach seen from Dow's Hill, Antigua

beaches.name: Galley Bay
beaches.tagline: Long west-coast beach with epic sunsets
beaches.summary: A long, wild west-coast beach with a more dramatic surf than most leeward bays. A romantic, resort-fronted stretch known for spectacular sunsets and a bird sanctuary lagoon behind the sand.
beaches.html:
Galley Bay is a long, open beach on the Five Islands peninsula, facing west into the Caribbean. Unlike the island's most sheltered bays, Galley Bay catches a livelier swell, so it can have gentle surf and a more dramatic, romantic feel. The combination of soft sand, palm-backed shoreline, and big west-facing skies makes its sunsets some of the most photographed in Antigua.

Behind the beach lies a brackish lagoon and a stretch of protected shoreline used by nesting sea turtles in season. The adults-only Galley Bay resort fronts part of the sand, but as with every beach in Antigua the shoreline itself is public, so you are free to walk the full length and swim.

The surf means swimming conditions vary: calm and inviting on settled days, choppier when the swell is up, so judge the water before going in. There is little public shade or facilities outside the resort, so come prepared. Galley Bay rewards visitors who want a quieter, more elemental beach and a front-row seat for sunset.

The beach is a short drive from St. John's on the Five Islands peninsula, and parking is limited near the public access. There is no lifeguard, so families with young children may prefer the calmer, more sheltered bays nearby. During turtle-nesting season, keep well clear of any marked nests, avoid bright lights on the beach after dark, and never disturb a nesting turtle. With its long, open sweep of sand, gentle surf, and uninterrupted western horizon, Galley Bay is best saved for late afternoon, when the light is at its most golden and the crowds are thin.

beaches.name: Gravenor Bay
beaches.tagline: Barbuda’s southern anchorage of reef and white sand
beaches.summary: A wide bay at the southern tip of Barbuda between Coco Point and Spanish Point, where white sand meets calm turquoise water laced with snorkel-ready reefs.
beaches.html:
Gravenor Bay scoops a wide, mile-and-a-half curve across the southern tip of Barbuda, its shoreline running east to west between Coco Point and Spanish Point. This is the bay that cruising sailors talk about for years afterward: a sheltered anchorage of glassy turquoise water, a long ribbon of white sand, and reefs that sit close enough to swim to from the beach. Check sea conditions before snorkelling; calm water is not assured.

The reefs are the headline. Coral heads scatter across the bay floor in clusters, and the unpolluted water keeps visibility high, so even casual snorkellers see reef fish, sea fans and the occasional ray drifting over the sand. Bring your own mask and fins, because there is no kiosk renting gear out here. If you are weighing up where to get in the water on the island, snorkelling around Antigua and Barbuda is at its most rewarding in quiet, reef-rich spots exactly like this one.

Gravenor Bay has residences overlooking it; the beach has no public facilities, no shade beyond what you carry, and no lifeguards, so come self-sufficient with water and sun cover. Most visitors arrive by boat as part of a wider exploration of Barbuda, often anchoring for a swim before continuing on. The peninsula running out to Spanish Point at the eastern end rewards a walk, with views back across the anchorage.

The easiest way to reach this corner of the island is on a guided Barbuda day trip, which handles the ferry or flight from Antigua and the local transport that scattered beaches like this one require. Every beach in Antigua and Barbuda is public by law, so the sand and the snorkelling are open to all who make the journey south.

beaches.name: Green Island
beaches.tagline: Uninhabited boat-access island and reefs
beaches.summary: An uninhabited offshore island reached only by boat, ringed with secluded white-sand coves and reefs. A protected, pristine spot for snorkeling, kitesurfing, and castaway-style seclusion.
beaches.html:
Green Island is a small, uninhabited island off the southeast coast of Antigua, reached only by boat. Its undeveloped shoreline is dotted with secluded white-sand coves and fringed with reefs, and because there are no roads or hotels, it offers a genuine castaway experience of pristine, near-empty beaches.

The island and its surrounding waters are part of a protected area, and the reefs make it a prime spot for snorkeling, with clear water, coral, and abundant fish. The shallow, flat-water lagoons on the protected side are also popular with kitesurfers and paddleboarders, while the quiet coves are perfect for swimming and simply doing nothing.

Getting there is half the adventure. Boats and catamaran tours run from the Long Bay and Nonsuch Bay area, and many snorkeling and sailing excursions include a stop here. Many trips combine the island with nearby Long Bay beach or the rock arch at Devil's Bridge. Bring everything you need, including water, food, and sun protection, since visitor services are limited. For seclusion, snorkeling, and untouched Caribbean scenery, Green Island is a special day trip.

The easiest way to visit is on an organized day trip or a chartered boat, which usually includes snorkel gear, drinks, and lunch, so you do not have to carry much yourself. There is no lifeguard and some shade, so a good hat and plenty of water are essential. Independent visitors can arrange a boat transfer from the Nonsuch Bay side. Whether you come to snorkel the reefs, kitesurf the flat-water lagoons, or simply find an empty cove and do nothing at all, Green Island offers one of the most genuine castaway experiences in Antigua, just a short boat ride from the east coast.

beaches.name: Half Moon Bay
beaches.tagline: National Park crescent with surf and calm corners
beaches.summary: A near-kilometre crescent of pale sand on the wild Atlantic east coast, protected as a National Park: surf and bodyboarding at the open end, calm swimming at the sheltered corner, and no resorts in sight.
beaches.html:
Half Moon Bay is widely considered one of the most beautiful beaches in Antigua, and it is protected as a National Park. A near-perfect crescent of pale, fine sand curves for almost a kilometer along the wild Atlantic east coast, backed by low scrub and framed by rocky headlands, with no large development to spoil the view.

The bay offers two beaches in one. The open, central section faces the Atlantic and catches a real swell, with surf and bodyboarding waves and a breeze that keeps it cooler than the leeward coast. The sheltered corner, protected by the reef and headland, stays much calmer and is the spot for safe swimming and snorkeling.

Its east-facing, Atlantic position means stronger currents in the open water and a seasonal risk of sargassum seaweed, so judge conditions and swim in the calm corner. Facilities are minimal, in keeping with its National Park status, so bring water and shade. Remote and unspoiled, Half Moon Bay rewards the longer drive to Antigua's eastern tip with raw, dramatic Caribbean beauty.

The beach is one of the furthest from V. C. Bird International Airport and the main resort areas, roughly a 45-minute drive to the southeastern tip near Long Bay, so it is best planned as a half-day trip rather than a quick stop. Parking is free in the lot, and there is no lifeguard, which makes the calm corner the only sensible place to swim when the Atlantic swell is up. Pack water, snacks, and an umbrella, since shade and services are sparse. It pairs well with the reef-protected, family-friendly Long Bay a little to the north. For its scenery alone, the sweeping crescent, the rolling surf, and the wild, empty feel, Half Moon Bay is many travelers' favorite beach on the island.

photo.alt: Half Moon Bay from the air, Antigua

beaches.name: Hawksbill Beach
beaches.tagline: Four coves and a turtle-shaped rock
beaches.summary: Four calm coves in one, named for an offshore rock shaped like a hawksbill turtle's beak. The quiet Five Islands peninsula has good rocky-point snorkeling and Antigua's only clothing-optional beach.
beaches.html:
Hawksbill is a cluster of four small beaches strung along the Five Islands peninsula, named for an offshore rock formation that resembles the beak of a hawksbill turtle. Each cove has its own character, from busy resort sand to secluded pockets, and the calm leeward water is clear and good for swimming and snorkeling around the rocky points.

The fourth and most remote of the beaches is Antigua's only clothing-optional (nudist) beach, reached by a short walk beyond the resort. The other beaches require clothing, though children under 16 are not allowed on resort property. As everywhere on the island the sand is public, even though the Hawksbill resort fronts the main beach, but access to the other three beaches is through Hawksbill Hotel Resort.

The peninsula setting gives Hawksbill a peaceful, away-from-it-all feel, with green headlands framing each bay and the distinctive turtle-shaped rock offshore. Snorkeling is good along the rocky edges where fish gather. Public facilities are limited outside the resort, so bring water and an umbrella, and the gentle west-coast sunsets are a fine way to end a visit.

To explore all four coves, start at Royal Palm Beach; the other three are accessed through Hawksbill Hotel Resort. There is no lifeguard, but the leeward water is usually calm. The beaches are a short drive from St. John's, with limited parking, so arrive earlier on busy days. Snorkelers should bring their own gear, since the best fish life clusters around the points rather than off the main beach. Quiet, scenic, and a little secret, Hawksbill rewards visitors who like to wander.

photo.alt: Sea Grapes Beach in Hawksbill Bay, Antigua

beaches.name: Hermitage Bay Beach
beaches.tagline: A hidden, calm-water cove on the sunset coast
beaches.summary: A hidden crescent of pale sand tucked into the green hills of Antigua's far west coast, where the Caribbean lies glassy and still and the sunsets glow straight off the water.
beaches.html:
Hermitage Bay is one of the most secluded beaches on Antigua's leeward coast, a small curve of pale sand with coarse grains and shells wrapped by wooded hillsides about 2.5 km (1.5 miles) north of Jolly Harbour. Because it faces west into the Caribbean and sits deep inside a sheltered cove, the water is generally calm and clear, though the resort sometimes posts a red flag, which makes it a dreamlike spot for an unhurried swim or a long float beneath the hills.

The bay is home to the Hermitage Bay resort, whose cottages climb the slope behind the sand, but as on every shoreline in the country the beach itself is public by law. Getting here is the catch: there is no easy roadside parking, so most visitors reach it by a rough off-road track or by boat, and the simplest land route runs through the resort itself. That difficulty is exactly what keeps the bay so quiet, even when busier beaches fill up.

Calm, transparent water makes Hermitage Bay a gentle place to swim, and the rocky edges of the cove are worth exploring slowly with a mask; for more ideas across the island, see our guide to snorkeling in Antigua. There are few facilities for casual visitors beyond what the resort provides, so treat this as a tranquil, bring-your-own kind of beach day rather than a service-heavy one.

The bay sits within easy reach of the Five Islands peninsula and the marina town of Jolly Harbour just to the south, so it slots neatly into a west-coast itinerary. Come for the morning calm and the soft afternoon light, and because this is a sunset-side bay, linger as the sky turns gold over the water before you head back.

facts.label: Parking
facts.value: Limited; most visitors arrive via a rough off-road track, by boat, or through the resort

beaches.name: Hodges Bay
beaches.tagline: Calm north-coast water and the gateway to Prickly Pear Island
beaches.summary: A calm, protected stretch of soft sand on Antigua's upscale north coast, with gentle Caribbean water that is ideal for families and an easy boat launch out to Prickly Pear Island.
beaches.html:
Hodges Bay sits on Antigua's north coast, facing the Atlantic. Conditions can vary, and the soft, pale sand shelves gently into shallow, protected shallows. It is a quietly upscale corner of the island, home to the Hodges Bay Resort and a cluster of smart villas, so the beach has a polished, residential feel rather than a busy resort-strip atmosphere.

The gentle, sheltered water makes Hodges Bay a genuinely good choice for families: young children can paddle safely, and unhurried swimming is the order of the day. The big draw beyond the sand is the water just offshore. Boats run from here out to Prickly Pear Island, a tiny uninhabited cay ringed by reef, where day trips combine snorkeling, swimming, and dining at XIV Beach Club. External guests must reserve, subject to availability and confirmation; the minimum spend is USD $400.00 for 1–6 persons. If you are weighing up where to base a north-coast beach day, livelier Dickenson Bay and its long resort strip lie a short drive west.

Hodges Bay works well as a calm-water alternative to the island's busier beaches, and it pairs naturally with the longer arc of Dickenson Bay Beach if you want to compare the two on the same trip. Keen snorkelers can build a day around the reefs offshore; see our guide to snorkeling in Antigua for where the clearest water and best coral sit.

A few practical notes. Every beach in Antigua is public by law, so access is free even where villas and the resort front the sand. There is no lifeguard, but the calm, gently shelving bay keeps conditions forgiving. Natural shade is limited away from the trees and resort grounds, so pack an umbrella for the middle of the day. The first resort boat to Prickly Pear departs at 11:00 a.m., and external guests need a confirmed reservation.

beaches.name: Jabberwock Beach
beaches.tagline: Antigua's prime kitesurfing and windsurfing beach
beaches.summary: A long, open ribbon of white sand on Antigua's breezy north coast, where steady trade winds make it the island's leading kitesurfing and windsurfing beach.
beaches.html:
Jabberwock Beach runs for roughly a mile along Antigua's north coast, a wide, open stretch of pale sand backed by sea grape and clusters of palms. It is exposed rather than sheltered, and that is the point: the same trade winds that other beaches are tucked away from blow steadily across Jabberwock most of the year. The result is Antigua's number one wind sport beach, where kitesurfers and windsurfers gather in force.

The wind season runs strongest from roughly December through June, when the steady on-shore to side-on breeze draws riders of every level. Beginners take lessons in the shallows while experienced kiters work the open water. Because the beach faces the breezier side of the island, the water has more chop than the calm leeward bays, so it is built for boards and sails rather than gentle paddling. For flat, protected water, the leeward shore around Dickenson Bay sits a short drive west.

Jabberwock is a natural, low-key spot with few facilities, which is part of its character. It is a favourite with locals at the weekend, who come for the space, the breeze, and picnics under the trees, and it is famously close to V. C. Bird International Airport, an easy first or last stop on a trip. Keen riders can plan a full day around the conditions with our guide to kitesurfing and windsurfing in Antigua.

A few practical notes. Every beach in Antigua is public by law, so access is free and parking is informal roadside. There is no lifeguard, and the open, wind-exposed water means stronger currents than the calm bays, so it suits confident swimmers and wind sport riders rather than small children. Natural shade is limited away from the trees, so bring an umbrella and plenty of water. Conditions are usually best when the trades pick up in the afternoon. For another wind spot, Dutchmans Bay Beach sits further along the same coast.

beaches.name: Johnson's Point
beaches.tagline: Calm, clear water and casual bars on the southwest coast
beaches.summary: A calm, shallow stretch of white sand on Antigua's southwest coast near Crab Hill, with clear turquoise water and a couple of casual beach bars. A relaxed local favorite for easy swimming and sunsets.
beaches.html:
Johnson's Point sits on Antigua's southwest Caribbean coast, just south of the village of Crab Hill and tucked between two of the island's prettiest stretches of sand, Ffryes Beach and Darkwood Beach. Because this leeward shore faces the Caribbean rather than the Atlantic, the water stays calm, clear, and warm, shelving gently from the white sand into shallow turquoise that is ideal for an unhurried swim.

This is a low-key, local-leaning beach rather than a resort strip. A couple of casual beach bars sit back from the sand, the kind of barefoot spots where you can settle in with a cold drink, fresh-grilled seafood, and reggae drifting across the bay. The relaxed pace and the absence of crowds are the whole appeal: most days you can find a quiet patch of sand and have the shallows largely to yourself.

Check the water conditions before swimming here, especially with children. Like all beaches in Antigua, it is public by law, so access is free even where the sand is fronted by villas. Natural shade is limited beyond the bars and a few sea-grape trees, so an umbrella helps in the middle of the day. There is no lifeguard, but the calm leeward water keeps conditions easy.

The beach is a short drive south of the Jolly Harbour marina village, which makes it simple to fold into a day of bar-hopping along the southwest coast. Because it faces west, late afternoon is the prize: the breeze drops, the water turns to glass, and the sun sets straight out over the Caribbean. Pair a swim here with neighboring Ffryes and Darkwood, and you have one of the most rewarding low-key beach circuits on the island.

beaches.name: Jolly Beach
beaches.tagline: One of Antigua's longest white-sand beaches
beaches.summary: One of Antigua's longest beaches: a wide, gently sloping ribbon of soft white sand on the calm southwest coast, with beach bars, watersports, and easy swimming. Lively but never overwhelming.
beaches.html:
Jolly Beach is one of the longest stretches of sand in Antigua, running for well over a kilometer along the calm southwest coast beside the Jolly Harbour marina village. The wide, soft, white-sand beach shelves gently into clear Caribbean water, making it a dependable choice for swimming, families, and long shoreline walks.

A large resort fronts part of the beach, and beach bars, restaurants, and watersports vendors line the sand, so you can rent a lounger, hire a paddleboard or kayak, or settle in for lunch and a swim. Despite the development, the sheer length of the beach means there is always room to spread out and find a quieter patch.

Because it faces southwest, the water is calm and the light is beautiful in the late afternoon. The nearby Jolly Harbour complex adds shops, a supermarket, and dining, so this is an easy base for a beach day with everything close at hand. Come early on cruise days for the calmest water and the pick of the loungers.

There is no lifeguard, but the wide, gently shelving beach and calm water make it one of the safer spots for families. Parking is free and plentiful at the public lots. Because Jolly Harbour has self-catering villas and apartments as well as resort rooms, the beach draws a mix of independent travelers and families who return day after day. If you want a single, fuss-free base with a long beach, easy swimming, watersports, and shops and restaurants all within walking distance, Jolly Beach is one of the most convenient choices on the southwest coast.

photo.alt: Jolly Beach and Jolly Harbour from the air, Antigua

beaches.name: Little Ffryes Beach
beaches.tagline: The hidden cove next to Ffryes
beaches.summary: A pocket-sized cove tucked just around the rocks from busier Ffryes Beach, with the same powder-soft sand and calm turquoise water, but a fraction of the crowd.
beaches.html:
Little Ffryes Beach is the quieter sibling of its famous neighbour. Hidden in a small cove on Antigua's southwest coast, just around a low rocky point from the popular Ffryes Beach, it offers the same fine white sand and clear turquoise shallows with far fewer people spread along it. If the main strand feels busy on a cruise-ship day, a short walk over the rocks brings you to a calmer pocket of shoreline that many visitors never bother to find.

The water here is sheltered and typically calm, in keeping with Antigua's leeward west coast, where the sea stays gentle and the swimming is easy. The cove is compact, so it has an intimate, almost private feel even when the wider Ffryes area is lively. Sunsets are a draw along this stretch of coast, and the modest size of Little Ffryes makes it a peaceful spot to watch the light fade over the Caribbean without jostling for a patch of sand.

Facilities are minimal, which is part of the appeal. Bring your own water, shade and snacks, since the cove itself has little in the way of amenities, though the restaurants and beach bars around the larger Ffryes Beach are only a short stroll away. The setting suits travellers who want to read, swim and unwind rather than chase activity. Like every beach on the island, it is public by law, so access is free.

Little Ffryes pairs naturally with a wider west-coast day. It sits within easy reach of Jolly Harbour and its marina, and forms part of the cluster of calm leeward coves that includes nearby Valley Church Beach. With a car you can hop between several of these beaches in a single afternoon, using Little Ffryes as the quiet escape when the more popular sands fill up.

facts.label: Parking
facts.value: Limited roadside parking near Ffryes Beach

beaches.name: Long Bay
beaches.tagline: Reef-protected turquoise water on the east point
beaches.summary: A reef-protected beach on the easternmost point of the island, where the Atlantic breeze meets calm, shallow, turquoise water. Excellent for families and some of the best shore snorkeling in Antigua.
beaches.html:
Long Bay sits at the easternmost point of Antigua, where a wide, healthy reef runs across the mouth of the bay and tames the Atlantic. The result is the best of both worlds: a refreshing east-coast breeze and views of open ocean, but calm, shallow, brilliantly turquoise water inside the reef that is generally sheltered for swimming, though conditions can change.

That protected, shallow water makes Long Bay one of the safest and most family-friendly beaches on the island, where children can wade and paddle far out in waist-deep turquoise. It also offers some of the finest shore-accessible snorkeling in Antigua: the reef is alive with coral and fish and lies within easy swimming distance of the sand.

The Pineapple Beach Club resort and a couple of beach bars sit behind the resort's quarter-mile beachfront, providing drinks, food, and lounger rentals, but the bay keeps a relaxed, low-key feel. Because it faces east, it can occasionally collect sargassum seaweed in season. With its calm water, vivid color, easy snorkeling, and pleasant breeze, Long Bay is a standout on the quieter east coast.

The drive out to the eastern point takes you well away from the busy west-coast resorts, so plan it as part of a day exploring the east, perhaps combined with a boat trip to Green Island or a visit to the dramatic rock arch at Devil's Bridge nearby. There is no lifeguard, but the reef-protected inner water is gentle and shallow. Bring your own snorkel gear, since the reef is the main attraction and lies within easy reach of the sand. For families who want safe, colorful water and great snorkeling without the crowds, Long Bay is one of the best beaches in Antigua.

beaches.name: Mamora Bay Beach
beaches.tagline: A sheltered golden-sand bay on a quiet peninsula
beaches.summary: A sheltered crescent of golden sand on the St James's Club peninsula, where calm, glassy water laps a palm-fringed bay on Antigua's quiet southeast coast.
beaches.html:
Mamora Bay sits on a secluded peninsula on the southeast coast, a short drive east of the historic harbours. The bay curves into a calm, palm-backed pocket of golden sand, and because it faces inward rather than out to the open Atlantic, the water stays remarkably sheltered and still. It is the kind of bay where you wade in slowly and the surface barely ripples, ideal for an easy swim or a long float with nothing but the tree line and a few small boats for company.

The beach shares its peninsula with the St James's Club resort, but like every shoreline in the country it is public by law. To reach it, drive out to the security gate at the peninsula entrance and park nearby; the staff there will point you to the path down to the sand. It is a low-key arrival rather than a roadside pull-off, so the bay tends to stay calm and uncrowded even when busier beaches fill up.

Calm, clear water makes Mamora Bay a natural spot for gentle paddling and non-motorized water sports, and the rocky edges of the bay reward a slow swim with a mask. If you want more bite from the sea, the peninsula's ocean-facing side picks up real surf, a striking contrast just a short walk away. For more snorkeling ideas across the island, see our guide to snorkeling in Antigua.

The bay pairs well with a day around English Harbour and the Georgian naval buildings at Nelson's Dockyard just to the west. Come in the morning for the calmest water and softest light, bring your own shade and water, and treat this as a tranquil stop rather than a facilities-heavy beach day.

facts.label: Parking
facts.value: Available near the peninsula security gate

beaches.name: Morris Bay
beaches.tagline: Peaceful south-coast bay below Curtain Bluff
beaches.summary: A quiet, scenic south-coast beach near Old Road with soft sand, calm water, and views toward Curtain Bluff. A peaceful spot for swimming and snorkeling away from the crowds.
beaches.html:
Morris Bay is a serene, picturesque beach on Antigua's south coast near Old Road village, just west of Carlisle Bay. The soft sand, calm water, and quiet atmosphere make it a peaceful escape from the busier beaches, with the dramatic headland of Curtain Bluff rising to one side.

The bay is sheltered and the water stays calm and clear, good for unhurried swimming and for snorkeling around the rocky edges and reef patches, where tropical fish gather. A small resort sits at one end, but the long beach has plenty of open, public sand to spread out on, and it rarely feels crowded.

Because it is a little off the main beach circuit, Morris Bay keeps a low-key, local feel. Facilities are limited, so bring water, snacks, and shade. Its calm water, scenic setting between green headlands, and reliable snorkeling make Morris Bay a rewarding stop for travelers exploring the quieter south coast around Old Road.

Parking is roadside and limited, and there is no lifeguard, though the sheltered bay stays gentle. The beach is an easy add-on to neighboring Carlisle Bay, which sits just to the east, so the two make a natural pair for a quiet day on the south coast. Bring your own snorkel gear and water shoes for the rocky edges where the fish gather. If you are based around English Harbour, Morris Bay is a short drive west and offers a calmer, emptier alternative to the busier beaches, ideal for travelers who simply want soft sand, clear water, and quiet.

beaches.name: Pigeon Point Beach
beaches.tagline: Calm, accessible beach by English Harbour
beaches.summary: An easy, family-friendly beach on Falmouth Harbour with calm, shallow water and two beach bars. The most accessible beach near English Harbour and a favorite for relaxed afternoons.
beaches.html:
Pigeon Point Beach sits in the sheltered bay of Falmouth Harbour, just a few minutes' drive from English Harbour and historic Nelson's Dockyard. As one of the most accessible beaches on the south coast, it is a reliable, easygoing choice, with calm, shallow water that is ideal for families with young children.

The beach is fringed with palms and backed by a couple of popular beach bars and restaurants serving drinks, seafood, and Caribbean lunches, which gives it a sociable, relaxed atmosphere. Loungers and umbrellas are usually available to rent, and the gentle, protected water makes it a comfortable spot to spend a full afternoon swimming and lazing.

Because of its calm water, easy access, food options, and proximity to the dockyard, Pigeon Point is a natural pairing with a morning of sightseeing in English Harbour. It can get busy on weekends and cruise days, but the friendly vibe and convenience keep it a perennial favorite for both visitors and locals.

Parking is free in the lot behind the beach, and there is no lifeguard, but the shallow, sheltered harbour water is about as gentle as it gets on the island. Pigeon Point works well as a base for exploring the historic south coast: spend the morning at Nelson's Dockyard, the afternoon on the sand, and the evening up at Shirley Heights for the famous Sunday sunset party. With two beach bars, easy water, and so much history on the doorstep, it is one of the most convenient and well-rounded beaches near English Harbour.

beaches.name: Pink Sand Beach (17 Mile Beach)
beaches.tagline: Miles of deserted pink-tinged Caribbean sand
beaches.summary: Barbuda's legendary pink-tinged beach: miles of soft, blush-colored sand and clear shallows, almost completely deserted. One of the Caribbean's most extraordinary and remote stretches of coastline.
beaches.html:
Barbuda's Pink Sand Beach, part of the vast strand known as 17 Mile Beach, is one of the most extraordinary beaches in the Caribbean. The sand carries a soft blush of pink, created by countless tiny fragments of pink coral and shell mixed into the white sand, and the effect is most striking in soft morning and evening light.

What truly sets it apart is its scale and emptiness. The beach runs for miles along Barbuda's sheltered western shore, fronting clear, shallow, calm water, and you can often walk for a very long way without seeing another person. Backed by the lagoon and the famous frigate bird sanctuary, it is a place of rare, unspoiled wilderness.

Barbuda lies about 30 miles north of Antigua and is reached by ferry or a short flight, then, for Low Bay, a transfer to the Codrington Lagoon Fisheries wharf and a pre-booked water taxi to the sand. Visit the nearby Frigate Bird Sanctuary by boat while you are there. There are very few facilities, so bring water, food, and sun protection. For sheer, remote, pink-tinged beauty, this beach is the jewel of Barbuda.

Most travelers experience Pink Sand Beach on a guided day trip from Antigua, which typically bundles the ferry or flight, a local guide, the frigate bird boat tour, and lunch, taking the logistics off your hands. If you visit independently, plan transfers in advance, since taxis and boats on Barbuda are limited and the island is sparsely populated. There is no lifeguard; water conditions differ between the seaward and lagoon sides, so check conditions before swimming. The pink hue is subtle rather than neon, most visible up close and in soft light, so keep expectations realistic and let the sheer scale and emptiness of the beach be the real wonder. It is unlike anywhere else in the country.

facts.value: Free (ferry or flight to reach Barbuda)

beaches.name: Rendezvous Bay
beaches.tagline: Secluded white-sand bay reached on foot or by boat
beaches.summary: A remote, undeveloped white-sand bay on the south coast, reached on foot, by boat or by four-wheel drive. The reward is a pristine, near-empty beach with calm, clear water and total seclusion.
beaches.html:
Rendezvous Bay is one of Antigua's great hidden beaches, a wide arc of soft white sand and calm, clear water on the south coast between Falmouth and Carlisle Bay. What sets it apart is its isolation: access by vehicle requires four-wheel drive, so it stays undeveloped, pristine, and often completely empty.

Reaching it is part of the appeal. Most visitors hike in over the hills from the English Harbour area, a roughly 30 to 45 minute walk on a rough trail, while others arrive by boat or kayak. The effort keeps the crowds away, and on many days you may have this beautiful beach almost to yourself.

The water can be calm, but the bay can also turn rough, so check conditions before swimming, with green hills and palm trees framing the sand. There are no facilities of any kind, so you must bring everything you need, including plenty of water, food, and sun protection, and carry out all your trash. For travelers willing to make the trek, Rendezvous Bay delivers a rare sense of seclusion and unspoiled Caribbean beauty.

If you hike, set off early to avoid the midday heat, wear sturdy shoes, and follow the trail that climbs from the Falmouth side; there is no lifeguard and no phone signal in places, so it is wise to go with others and tell someone your plans. Many visitors take the easier option of a boat or kayak from the English Harbour area, which doubles as a scenic mini-excursion. Either way, the payoff is the same: a pristine, undeveloped beach that feels a world away from the resorts, and on a quiet day, the sense that you have found a corner of Antigua almost nobody else reaches.

facts.value: Possible along the rough approach; walk in from there

beaches.name: Runaway Bay
beaches.tagline: The calm, low-key neighbor of Dickenson Bay
beaches.summary: A long, quiet stretch of pale sand just south of Dickenson Bay, with the same calm Caribbean water but a fraction of the crowds. A laid-back local favorite for swimming and sunset walks.
beaches.html:
Runaway Bay runs along the northwest coast immediately south of busier Dickenson Bay, the two beaches separated only by a low headland. It offers the same warm, shallow, west-facing Caribbean water but with far fewer people, which makes it a quiet alternative for travelers who want calm swimming without the resort bustle.

The sand is soft and pale, and a handful of casual beach bars and a couple of small hotels dot the shore. Because the bay is sheltered and shelves gently, the water stays calm and clear, good for unhurried swims and for letting children paddle. Local families come here at weekends for the relaxed atmosphere.

Shade is limited away from the bars, so bring an umbrella. The beach faces due west, so this is one of the better spots near Dickenson Bay to settle in for sunset. Some erosion over the years has narrowed sections of the sand, but the long, open feel and easy access keep Runaway Bay a reliable, low-key choice.

Because the two beaches sit side by side, many visitors combine them, swimming and people-watching at lively Dickenson Bay, then walking the short distance to Runaway Bay for a quieter stretch of the same calm water. Parking is simply roadside, and there is no lifeguard, though the sheltered, gently shelving bay keeps conditions easy. With watersports vendors, bars, and restaurants all within a short walk, Runaway Bay gives you the convenience of the resort strip without the crowds, which is exactly why locals favor it at weekends.

beaches.name: Spanish Point
beaches.tagline: Where the Caribbean meets the Atlantic at the edge of Barbuda
beaches.summary: A wild, windswept peninsula at the far southeast tip of Barbuda, where a thin ribbon of sand separates the glassy Caribbean from the open Atlantic surf, with reefs offshore and a ruined old stone tower a short way inland near the bay.
beaches.html:
Spanish Point sits at the extreme southeast corner of Barbuda, a slender finger of land marking the eastern end of Gravenor Bay. It is one of the most dramatic spots on the island precisely because of where it stands: the calm, pale-turquoise Caribbean laps one side of the peninsula while the darker, restless Atlantic rolls in on the other. Walk the narrow neck of sand and you can feel both seas at once, a quiet lagoon-like shore on your right and a churning open ocean on your left.

This is rugged, remote country. There are no resorts, no beach bars, and no crowds here, just low scrub, weathered rock, and scattered coral, while the skeleton of an old stone tower stands a short way inland near the bay. Offshore reefs break the Atlantic swell and create patches of sheltered water where the snorkelling can be rewarding when conditions are calm. Because the point faces the windward side of the island, the eastern shore is often breezy and choppy, while the Gravenor Bay side stays noticeably gentler.

Most visitors reach Spanish Point as part of a wider Barbuda outing, pairing it with the famous pink-sand stretches and a stop at the Frigate Bird Sanctuary. A guided Barbuda day trip is the easiest way to fold it into a single visit, since the peninsula lies well off the main settlement and the track out can be rough. Bring water, sun protection, and sturdy footwear for the coral and rock.

Come for the sense of standing at the edge of the island, with the Caribbean Sea and Atlantic Ocean meeting beneath your feet and barely another soul in sight. Spanish Point rewards travellers who like their beaches raw, empty, and a little bit untamed rather than groomed and serviced.

beaches.name: Turner's Beach
beaches.tagline: Palm-backed beach with snorkeling and a bar
beaches.summary: A friendly, palm-backed beach on the southwest tip with calm water, good shore snorkeling, and the well-known Turner's beach bar. A relaxed spot with Montserrat on the horizon.
beaches.html:
Turner's Beach lies near the southwest tip of Antigua, a relaxed crescent of pale sand backed by palms and sea-grape trees. The calm, clear Caribbean water and the easygoing atmosphere make it a favorite with both visitors and locals, and it pairs naturally with nearby Darkwood Beach just up the coast.

The beach is best known for Turner's, a long-running beach bar and restaurant on the sand that serves cold drinks, fresh seafood, and Caribbean lunches, and rents out loungers and umbrellas. Rocky patches and seagrass close to shore give it some of the better casual snorkeling on this stretch of coast, with reef fish around the edges of the bay.

Facing southwest, Turner's has calm water and good light, with the volcanic island of Montserrat visible across the channel on clear days. It can get busy when cruise excursions arrive, but the length of sand keeps it comfortable. With food, drinks, loungers, and snorkeling all in one easy spot, Turner's is a dependable full-day beach.

Parking is free, either roadside or in a small lot, and there is no lifeguard, though the sheltered water is gentle and good for swimming. Turner's sits a short drive south of Jolly Harbour, so it slots neatly into a southwest-coast circuit alongside Darkwood Beach just to the north. Bring water shoes for the rockier snorkeling spots, and an umbrella if you want guaranteed shade beyond the palms. Friendly, scenic, and well equipped without being overdeveloped, Turner's is the kind of beach where you can happily lose a whole day.

beaches.name: Two Foot Bay
beaches.tagline: Barbuda's untamed Atlantic coast of cliffs and caves
beaches.summary: A wild, windswept shore on Barbuda's remote northeast coast, where limestone cliffs and caves meet open Atlantic surf. This is a beach for explorers, not loungers.
beaches.html:
Two Foot Bay sits on the rugged northeast coast of Barbuda, facing the open Atlantic inside Two Foot Bay National Park. This is one of the wildest stretches of shoreline in the whole country: low limestone cliffs rise behind a coarse, pale shore, the surf rolls in with real energy, and there is no resort, though Hillside View Bar & Grill serves lunch at Two Foot Bay. The appeal is raw nature and history, not easy swimming.

The bay is best known for its caves. Indian Cave, set into the cliffs above the shore, holds the only petroglyphs left on Barbuda by the island's First Peoples, carved among the stalactites and stalagmites of a multi-chamber passage that climbs toward ocean views. The dramatic Darby Cave, a vast collapsed sinkhole ringed by bush a few miles inland, is usually paired with Two Foot Bay on a guided walk, and a local guide is well worth arranging to find the petroglyphs and read the landscape.

Because this is the Atlantic side of the island, conditions are breezy and the water can be choppy, with currents stronger than on Barbuda's calm western beaches, and seasonal sargassum can wash up at times. It is a place for beachcombing, birdwatching in the surrounding bushland, and cave exploration rather than long swims, so take care and watch the surf if you do go in.

Getting here is part of the adventure. Two Foot Bay is reached by a rough track from Codrington, Barbuda's only village, so a 4x4 or a tour with a local driver is the practical way in, and Hillside View Bar & Grill serves catered tour lunches. Bring water, sturdy shoes, and sun protection. Most visitors fold it into a wider Barbuda day trip, pairing the caves and cliffs with the famous pink-sand beaches and the frigate bird sanctuary on the lagoon. For travelers who want the empty, untamed face of the Caribbean, few places deliver as completely.

beaches.name: Valley Church Beach
beaches.tagline: Powder sand and glowing turquoise shallows
beaches.summary: A dazzling stretch of powder-white sand and pale turquoise shallows on the southwest coast. Often called one of Antigua's prettiest beaches, with calm water ideal for families.
beaches.html:
Valley Church Beach is a showstopper: a wide ribbon of fine, powder-white sand meeting astonishingly pale, turquoise shallows on the calm southwest coast. The water is so clear and the colors so vivid that it regularly appears on lists of Antigua's most beautiful beaches. It sits just north of Ffryes Beach, south of Jolly Harbour.

The shallow, gently shelving water can be inviting for swimming and families, but check conditions before entering: currents can be deceptively strong. A popular beach bar, The Nest, sits behind the sand serving drinks and food, and loungers are usually available to rent.

The beach can get busy on cruise days because tour operators bring groups here for its looks and its easy water, so come early for the calmest, emptiest conditions and the best light. Natural shade is limited beyond the bar and a few sea-grape trees, so bring an umbrella. For sheer Caribbean postcard beauty, Valley Church is hard to beat, but check conditions carefully before swimming and follow warnings.

Parking is free at the lot and roadside, and the beach is an easy drive south of Jolly Harbour. There is no lifeguard, but the shallow, calm water is among the most forgiving on the island for young swimmers. Snorkelers can explore the rocks at either end of the bay, where small fish gather. Because Valley Church and Ffryes are close by, the smartest plan is to spend the morning on the quieter, brighter sands of Valley Church, then drift over to Ffryes for sunset, giving you the best of two of Antigua's prettiest beaches in a single day.

beaches.name: Willoughby Bay
beaches.tagline: Antigua’s quiet white-sand southeast bay
beaches.summary: A large, quiet bay on Antigua’s southeast coast with soft white sand and generally calm, partly reef-sheltered water. Undeveloped and uncrowded, it is a relaxed spot for swimming, snorkelling and paddleboarding.
beaches.html:
Willoughby Bay is a large, tranquil bay on Antigua’s southeast coast, fringed by soft white sand and backed by gently rolling, bush-covered hills. A reef across much of the bay’s mouth helps soften the open ocean, so the water close to shore is generally calm and easy, which makes Willoughby Bay a relaxed place to swim, snorkel or take a paddleboard out over the shallows rather than a wild surf beach.

The bay stays remarkably uncrowded, even in high season. There are no rows of loungers, no beach bars lining the sand, and rarely more than a handful of people walking the shore. That emptiness is exactly the draw. The white sands of Crawl Bay beach, the calm water, and the green hills behind it make Willoughby Bay feel genuinely undeveloped, a quiet contrast to the polished resort beaches elsewhere on the island. Like every beach in Antigua, it is public by law, so the whole shoreline is yours to explore.

Like the rest of Antigua’s windward side, this coast catches the easterly trade winds, so you may feel a steady breeze along the shore even when the water near the beach stays settled. It is worth glancing at the day’s conditions before a longer swim, but most of the time the reef-sheltered shallows here are gentle and welcoming. Bring your own shade, water and snacks, as there are no facilities on the sand.

Willoughby Bay sits just east of English Harbour, with travel time varying by where you visit the bay, which makes it easy to pair a visit here with the island’s naval heritage and sheltered yachting bays. Come for soft sand, calm water, and the quiet of a coast that most visitors never see.
